## 9. Testing

`npm run test:environment` runs all six headless suites (IBL, probes, sky, time of day, night,
physical atmosphere).

- **`npm run test:sky`** — 14 headless checks (U1–U13 + the §8 error table). The gradient refactor
  is numerically inert to 1e-6; the bake kernel and the skybox carry byte-identical `sampleSky`
  bodies; every composed module parses; Preetham is monotone in turbidity and elevation and finite
  over 512 directions × 32 solar elevations; the CPU sun-radiance mirror matches the WGSL's own
  constants; `writeParams` allocates zero bytes; source bindings stay in the reserved 14–17 range.
- **`npm run test:sky:gpu`** — 13 numeric checks on a real device (headless Chrome; or open
  `/test/environment-gpu/` in a browser). Measured sun-disc radius vs `sunAngularRadius` within one
  pixel, skybox and bake against the CPU mirror, cube-edge continuity, `cheapSky: 1` against the
  pre-1.1 module, and the no-stale-mip source swap.
- **`npm run test:tod`** — headless celestial and integration checks: solar symmetry, polar
  day/night, the CPU radiance mirror, exclusive shadow-slot ownership and call order, sunset
  intensity, angular re-bake cadence at 1× and 1000×, lunar phase/illumination, normalized
  directions, zero typed-array allocation, `out` semantics, and named config errors. See
  [`time-of-day.md`](./time-of-day.md) §10.
- **`npm run test:night`** — celestial transforms, magnitude/flux, fixed-pixel sprite energy,
  Lommel–Seeliger lunar photometry, composite renaming, B−V colour, air-mass scintillation,
  by-reference catalogue upload, named errors, and WGSL parsing. See
  [`night-sky.md`](./night-sky.md) §8.
- **`npm run test:atmosphere`** — physical transmittance and wavelength ordering, the known vertical
  Rayleigh integral, phase normalization, LUT mappings, sky/composite binding propagation, named
  errors, and WGSL parsing. See [`atmosphere.md`](./atmosphere.md) §10.

`npm run test:environment` — 12 headless checks for the IBL half (U1–U10 + config validation):
cube-face convention, equirect round-trip, solid-angle exactness, SH packing order, ringing clamp,
constant-environment energy, rotation consistency, BRDF LUT endpoints, WGSL parse + binding budget,
the material hook, and the backtick guard.

The IBL GPU integration set (white furnace, fireflies, mirror fidelity) is still unwritten — see
[`lighting-ibl-design.md`](../lighting-ibl-design.md) §10 T1–T6.

docs.title: Environment — Shader & Buffer Reference
docs.text:
# Environment — Shader & Buffer Reference

Everything the GPU side of `null-graph/environment` touches: the bind-group map, the exact byte
layout of every buffer and texture, the WGSL functions the material bridge injects, and the
conventions a custom shader has to match to interoperate.

Usage-level docs: [`environment.md`](./environment.md) ·
Physical atmosphere: [`atmosphere.md`](./atmosphere.md) ·
Architecture: [`lighting-ibl-design.md`](../lighting-ibl-design.md)

---

## 1. The bind-group map

Core WebGPU guarantees **four** bind groups (`maxBindGroups: 4`) and NullGraph spends all four.
Indirect lighting therefore lives **inside group 2 alongside the lights** — there is no fifth group
on the baseline device.

| Group | Owner | Bindings |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | engine | `0` camera uniform · `1` instance/ECS storage |
| 1 | material | `0` sampler · `1..n` textures · `n+1` params uniform |
| **2** | **lights + environment** | `0–2` lights · **`3–6` environment** |
| 3 | shadows | `0` atlas · `1` comparison sampler · `2` params · `3–4` view/slot tables |

### 1.1 Group 2 in detail

```wgsl
// LightSystem — bindings 0..2 (clustered-forward; `standard` uses 0 only)
@group(2) @binding(0) var<storage, read> globalLights: array<Light>;
@group(2) @binding(1) var<storage, read> clusterGrid:  array<Cluster>;
@group(2) @binding(2) var<storage, read> lightIndices: array<u32>;

// EnvironmentSystem — bindings 3..6
@group(2) @binding(3) var envSampler:  sampler;
@group(2) @binding(4) var envSpecular: texture_cube<f32>;
@group(2) @binding(5) var brdfLUT:     texture_2d<f32>;
@group(2) @binding(6) var<uniform> env: EnvParams;
```

Bindings **7–13 are reserved** for Phase 2 (probe volumes, reflection probes) — see
[`lighting-ibl-design.md`](../lighting-ibl-design.md) §4.4 for the full allocation and the
per-stage resource counts against core limits. A new subsystem that claims a binding without
updating that table is spending someone else's budget.

**One owner builds the group.** `EnvironmentSystem.applyToBatch(batch, lights)` concatenates
`lights.getBindGroupEntries()` with its own. Calling `lights.applyToBatch(batch)` separately
overwrites the whole group; the environment throws if it detects that.

---

## 2. Buffer & texture layouts

### 2.1 `EnvParams` — 44 floats, 176 bytes, group 2 binding 6

```wgsl
struct EnvParams {
    shR: array<vec4<f32>, 3>,   // floats  0..11   SH-L2 red,   9 coeffs packed 3-per-vec4
    shG: array<vec4<f32>, 3>,   // floats 12..23   green
    shB: array<vec4<f32>, 3>,   // floats 24..35   blue
    rotation: vec4<f32>,        // floats 36..39   .xyz reserved; .w = yaw radians
    intensity: f32,             // float  40
    specularMip: f32,           // float  41       prefilterMips - 1
    horizonFade: f32,           // float  42
    _pad: f32,                  // float  43
};
```

**This buffer has two writers, and the split matters.**

| Floats | Owner | Written by |
|---|---|---|
| `0..35` (the SH block) | **GPU** | the SH projection kernel → `copySHToParams()` |
| `36..43` (the tail) | **CPU** | `setRotation`, `setIntensity`, construction |

The CPU-side write is deliberately **partial** — offset `36*4`, length 8 floats. A full-struct write
would clobber the projected coefficients with the CPU's stale zeros every time someone nudged the
intensity, and the symptom is "the environment goes black when I move a slider."

`setRawSH()` is the one path that deliberately writes floats `0..35`, because there the CPU *is*
the source.

#### The SH packing (§7.3)

WGSL uniform arrays stride to 16 bytes per element, so `array<vec3<f32>, 9>` would cost 144 bytes
per channel. Packing 3 coefficients per `vec4` costs 48 and unpacks in three loads:

```
coefficient k of a channel lives at   channelBase + (k / 3) * 4 + (k % 3)
                                      ^^^^^^^^^^^   0 (R) · 12 (G) · 24 (B)
```

```wgsl
fn shCoeffR(k: u32) -> f32 { return env.shR[k / 3u][k % 3u]; }
```

The twelfth slot of each `vec4` is unused and written as `0`. `envMath.packSHChannel` is the CPU
mirror, and the SH projection kernel writes this **exact layout** so the transport is one copy
(§3.3).

### 2.2 The SH staging buffer — 36 floats, group 0 binding 1 of the projection kernel

```wgsl
@group(0) @binding(1) var<storage, read_write> shOut: array<f32, 36>;
```

**36, not 27.** The natural output would be 9 `vec3` interleaved, but that would need a repack
before it could reach the uniform. Writing the packed `EnvParams` layout directly makes the
transport a single `copyBufferToBuffer(shBuffer, 0, envParamsBuffer, 0, 144)`.

### 2.3 Textures

| Texture | Format | Size | Usage | Views |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| source cube | `rgba16float` | `sourceSize²` × 6, full mip chain | `TEXTURE_BINDING \| STORAGE_BINDING` | `cube` (sample) + per-mip `2d-array` (write) |
| specular cube | `rgba16float` | `2^(mips+1)`² × 6, `prefilterMips` levels | `TEXTURE_BINDING \| STORAGE_BINDING` | `cube` (sample) + per-mip `2d-array` (write) |
| BRDF LUT | `rg16float` | `lutSize²` | `TEXTURE_BINDING \| STORAGE_BINDING` | `2d` |

**Why `rgba16float` and not `rgba32float`.** `rgba16float` is a core storage format *and* core
filterable. `rgba32float` needs the `float32-filterable` feature and silently loses linear sampling
without it — which would break the roughness-mip interpolation. The config throws if you ask for it.

**Two views of one texture** is the crux of the bake: a cube view to sample from, a per-mip
`2d-array` view to `textureStore` into. Same pattern as `HiZPyramid`, one dimension up.

### 2.4 The environment sampler

```ts
{ magFilter: 'linear', minFilter: 'linear', mipmapFilter: 'linear',
  addressModeU: 'clamp-to-edge', addressModeV: 'clamp-to-edge' }
```

`mipmapFilter: 'linear'` is load-bearing — the specular lookup interpolates **between roughness
mips**, and with `'nearest'` a roughness sweep steps visibly at each mip boundary.

### 2.5 The sky params array — `4 + source.paramFloats` floats

One flat `array<f32>` layout, read at **identical indices** by both consumers of the sky
([`environment-sky-design.md`](../environment-sky-design.md) §4.5). The 16-float
`SkyParams` *uniform* this replaced is gone: it described one hardcoded gradient, and a second sky
model would have needed a second struct.

| Float | Field | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | `exposure` | multiplies the skybox only, never the bake |
| 1 | `yaw` | the environment rotation — the same one the SH and specular lookups use (§4.5) |
| 2 | `blurMip` | prefiltered-cube mip. **Read only when `cheapSky` is 1** |
| 3 | `cheapSky` | `0` (default) evaluate `sampleSky` per pixel · `1` sample the prefiltered cube |
| 4..N | source params | written by `SkySource.writeParams(out, base)` with `base == 4` |

The stride comes from `source.paramFloats` — sized by demand, not by a cap
(design-principles §10). It is fixed when the sky batch is created; a source that changes
`paramFloats` after `setSky` is a named error (§8 of [`environment.md`](./environment.md)).

Two buffers carry this same layout, which is the point:

```wgsl
// skybox fragment — the batch storage buffer, bound by createBatch at group 0 binding 1
@group(0) @binding(1) var<storage, read> skyParams: array<f32>;

// Stage-A bake kernel — a system-owned buffer with the identical contents
@group(0) @binding(0) var<storage, read> skyParams: array<f32>;
```

`createBatch` binds `batch.storageBuffer` at group 0 binding 1 unconditionally, and `layout:'auto'`
prunes unused bindings — so a shader that ignores it makes `createBindGroup` throw. The skybox
therefore puts its actual parameters there. The binding is genuinely used, not an anti-prune trick.
On the bake side the mirror image applies: a source with `paramFloats === 0` must not reference
`skyParams` at all, and the system then omits the binding.

### 2.6 Sky-batch group 2 — and the reserved source range

The skybox batch has its **own** group-2 bind group: no lights, no probes, no BRDF LUT.

```wgsl
@group(2) @binding(3)  var envSampler:  sampler;              // always
@group(2) @binding(4)  var envSpecular: texture_cube<f32>;    // always — the cheapSky lookup
@group(2) @binding(14) var skySrcCube:  texture_cube<f32>;    // EquirectSky, via getSkyboxBindEntries
@group(2) @binding(15) var skySrcSampler: sampler;

// AtmosphereSky uses the same reserved source range instead:
@group(2) @binding(14) var sky_atm_trans:   texture_2d<f32>;
@group(2) @binding(15) var sky_atm_view:    texture_2d<f32>;
@group(2) @binding(16) var sky_atm_sampler: sampler;
```

**Bindings 14–17 are reserved for sky sources** and collide with nothing, because bindings 0–13 of
a fully-featured *material* (lights, IBL, probes) are never present on this batch. That separation
is why the evaluator costs **zero** material bindings — the constraint the whole seam is built
around ([`environment-sky-design.md`](../environment-sky-design.md) §4.3). Pinned by U11.

---

## 3. The WGSL contract

### 3.1 The two functions

`getShaderLayout()` returns `{ wgslStructs, wgslLogic }`. The logic half declares exactly these:

```wgsl
/** Cosine-convolved irradiance at worldPos with normal N, divided by PI.
 *  Multiply by albedo (and kD) for the diffuse indirect term. */
fn getIndirectDiffuse(worldPos: vec3<f32>, N: vec3<f32>) -> vec3<f32>;

/** Pre-integrated specular radiance for the reflection lobe, already including the split-sum
 *  BRDF term — the caller multiplies by nothing but occlusion. */
fn getIndirectSpecular(worldPos: vec3<f32>, N: vec3<f32>, V: vec3<f32>,
                       roughness: f32, F0: vec3<f32>) -> vec3<f32>;
```

**Both take `worldPos`, and Phase 1 ignores it.** That is deliberate: Phase 2 re-emits these same
two signatures against a probe volume, so swapping global IBL for spatially-varying probes costs
**zero material edits**. A contract that omitted the parameter would force a rewrite at exactly the
point where the code has the most users.

### 3.2 How a material consumes them

`ShaderConfig.indirect` is optional. Present, the PBR fragment's ambient becomes:

```wgsl
let F_ibl  = fresnelSchlickRoughness(max(dot(N, V), 0.0), F0, roughness);
let kD_ibl = (vec3<f32>(1.0) - F_ibl) * (1.0 - metallic);
let ambient = (kD_ibl * albedo * getIndirectDiffuse(in.worldPos, N)
               + getIndirectSpecular(in.worldPos, N, V, roughness, F0)) * ao;
```

Absent, it is the original `vec3<f32>(0.3) * albedo * ao`, byte-for-byte. Lambert and Toon take the
diffuse half only.

`fresnelSchlickRoughness` is supplied by `wgslStructs` — `PBR_MATH_WGSL` has `fresnelSchlick` but
not the roughness-aware form, and the environment adds it rather than editing the shared chunk.

### 3.3 Name-collision discipline

The injected logic uses **suffixed** copies of the shared math — `shBasisL2Env`, `rotateYEnv` —
because it is composed into a material module that does *not* include `ENV_MATH_WGSL`. `PI` is
**not** redeclared; the PBR chunk set owns it.

If you write a custom fragment that composes this layout, you must supply `PI` and a `VertexOut`
with `worldPos` / `worldNormal` / `uv` / `ecsColor`.

### 3.4 The sky contract — `ShaderSkyLayout`

A third `{ wgslStructs, wgslLogic }` pair, injected into the **bake kernel** and the **skybox
fragment** rather than into a material. `SkySource.getShaderLayout(base)` returns it, and its logic
half must declare exactly these two:

```wgsl
/** Radiance from world-space direction `dir` (normalized), linear HDR, in the scene-relative
 *  unit where 1.0 is a white Lambertian surface in direct midday sun. Must be finite and
 *  non-negative for EVERY unit vector — including straight down. */
fn sampleSky(dir: vec3<f32>) -> vec3<f32>;

/** The sun disc's colour at solar elevation `elevDeg`, WITHOUT its angular extent — what a
 *  directional light matching this sky should be tinted. Phase 2's CPU clock mirrors this
 *  function and nothing else; Phase 4 replaces the body with a transmittance LUT. */
fn skySunRadiance(elevDeg: f32) -> vec3<f32>;
```

**One evaluator, both consumers.** The same `wgslLogic` string goes into `buildSourceCubeWGSL` and
`buildSkyWGSL`, so the sky you are *lit by* and the sky you *see* are the same function by
construction rather than by review. U2 asserts the two carry byte-identical bodies; T2 asserts the
device agrees.

Three rules, each pinned by a test because each has bitten someone:

| Rule | Why | Test |
|---|---|---|
| Do not declare `PI` | the bake preamble (`ENV_MATH_WGSL`) and the material chunks both own it | U7 |
| Prefix every helper `sky_` | so a Phase 3 composite can rename without collision | U7 |
| No backtick anywhere | it terminates the JS template literal carrying it (§6) | U8 |

**The one sanctioned divergence.** A source backed by the source cube cannot sample the cube it is
writing, so `EquirectSky` supplies `getBakeShaderLayout()` — the bake facet reads the 2D equirect
through `dirToEquirectUV`, the skybox facet reads the baked cube at mip 0. Analytic sources omit it
and share a single body. Any *other* divergence between the two facets is a bug the seam exists to
prevent.

Params are addressed relative to `base` (always `4`, past the header of §2.5):

```ts
class MySky implements SkySource {
    readonly name = 'MySky';
    readonly paramFloats = 8;
    getShaderLayout(base: number) {
        return { wgslStructs: '', wgslLogic: `
fn sampleSky(dir: vec3<f32>) -> vec3<f32> {
    return vec3<f32>(skyParams[${base}], skyParams[${base + 1}], skyParams[${base + 2}]);
}
fn skySunRadiance(elevDeg: f32) -> vec3<f32> { return vec3<f32>(1.0); }
` };
    }
    writeParams(out: Float32Array, base: number) { out[base] = this.r; /* no allocation (U10) */ }
}
```

---

## 4. Conventions a custom shader must match

### 4.1 The cube-face convention

```wgsl
fn faceDirection(face: u32, uv: vec2<f32>) -> vec3<f32> {
    let c = uv * 2.0 - 1.0;
    switch face {
        case 0u: { return normalize(vec3<f32>( 1.0, -c.y, -c.x)); }   // +X
        case 1u: { return normalize(vec3<f32>(-1.0, -c.y,  c.x)); }   // -X
        case 2u: { return normalize(vec3<f32>( c.x,  1.0,  c.y)); }   // +Y
        case 3u: { return normalize(vec3<f32>( c.x, -1.0, -c.y)); }   // -Y
        case 4u: { return normalize(vec3<f32>( c.x, -c.y,  1.0)); }   // +Z
        default: { return normalize(vec3<f32>(-c.x, -c.y, -1.0)); }   // -Z
    }
}
```

One wrong sign mirrors the environment in a way that looks entirely plausible until a recognizable
feature shows up in a reflection. `envMath.faceDirection` is the CPU mirror; test **U1** pins all
six against known directions and every corner's octant.

### 4.2 Per-texel solid angle — use the exact form

```wgsl
fn areaElement(x: f32, y: f32) -> f32 { return atan2(x * y, sqrt(x * x + y * y + 1.0)); }

// texel spans [x0,x1]×[y0,y1] in face-local [-1,1] coords
Ω = areaElement(x0,y0) - areaElement(x0,y1) - areaElement(x1,y0) + areaElement(x1,y1)
```

The tempting midpoint form `(4/size²)/(s²+t²+1)^1.5` is a *differential* approximation that
converges only as O(1/size²) — measured, it over-counts the sphere by **0.38 % at size 8**, which is
exactly the mip the SH projection reads. That error lands directly in the irradiance as lost or
gained energy. The exact form sums to `4π` at any size; **U3** asserts `1e-4`, a tolerance the
midpoint form cannot reach.

A uniform `4π/384` weight is worse still — a cube's corner texels subtend markedly less than its
centre ones, so a flat weight tilts the whole irradiance field toward the corners.

### 4.3 SH basis order

```
[ 1, y, z, x, xy, yz, 3z²−1, xz, x²−y² ]
```

with the L2 normalization constants folded in, and the **cosine-convolution constants**
(`A0 = π`, `A1 = 2π/3`, `A2 = π/4`) applied at projection time — so the stored value *is*
irradiance and a debug readout is directly interpretable.

### 4.4 Clamp the SH evaluation

```wgsl
return max(c, vec3<f32>(0.0)) * env.intensity;
```

Not cosmetic. An L2 projection of a high-contrast environment **rings**, and the negative lobe
appears as black patches on surfaces facing away from the dominant light — a bug that reads as
"shadows in the wrong place." **U5** constructs exactly that environment and asserts the raw
evaluation goes negative while the shipped one does not.

### 4.5 Rotation applies to both halves

`env.rotation.w` (yaw) is applied to the normal before the SH lookup **and** to the reflection
vector before the cube sample. Rotating one and not the other is a common bug; the skybox reads the
same yaw from its own params so all three agree.

---

## 5. The bake kernels

| Stage | Entry | Dispatch | Bindings (group 0) |
|---|---|---|---|
| A source cube | `buildSourceCubeWGSL(skyLayout)` | `(size/8, size/8, 6)` | `0` sky params (omitted when `paramFloats === 0`), `2` dst, `3+` source-owned (EquirectSky's texture + sampler) |
| B mip chain | `buildCubeMipWGSL()` | `(dim/8, dim/8, 6)` per mip | `0` src cube, `1` dst mip, `2` sampler |
| C prefilter | `buildPrefilterWGSL({level, prefilterMips, samples, srcSize})` | `(dim/8, dim/8, 6)` per mip | `0` src cube, `1` sampler, `2` dst mip |
| D BRDF LUT | `buildBRDFLUTWGSL({samples})` | `(lutSize/8, lutSize/8, 1)` | `0` dst LUT |
| SH | `buildSHProjectWGSL()` | `(1, 1, 1)` | `0` src as `2d-array` at the 8×8 mip, `1` `shOut` |

`gid.z` is the cube face throughout. All entry points are `cs_main`.

### 5.1 Firefly suppression in the prefilter

```wgsl
let saTexel  = 4.0 * PI / (6.0 * SRC_SIZE * SRC_SIZE);
let saSample = 1.0 / (f32(SAMPLE_COUNT) * pdf);
let mip = 0.5 * log2(saSample / saTexel);
color += textureSampleLevel(srcCube, srcSamp, L, mip).rgb * NdotL;
```

Sampling the source mip whose texel solid angle matches the sample's (Karis) is what stops a single
bright texel — a sun disc — surviving as a swarm of hard dots at mid roughness. Remove it and the
artifact is immediate and obvious; **T2** measures the variance rather than trusting the eye.

Mip 0 short-circuits to a straight copy: roughness 0 is a mirror, and importance-sampling it only
adds noise.

### 5.2 Why the SH projection is one workgroup

WGSL has **no `atomic<f32>`**, so "every texel atomically accumulates into nine coefficients" does
not exist. Rather than build a two-pass reduction, the projection reads the source cube's **8×8
mip** — 6 faces × 64 texels = 384 samples — which fits one 64-thread workgroup with a tree reduction
in workgroup memory. Irradiance is a very low-frequency signal, so 8×8 is ample.

---

## 6. The authoring hazard: backticks

Every WGSL generator here is a **JavaScript template literal**. A backtick inside a WGSL comment
*terminates the string*, and everything after it is parsed as TypeScript — producing a cascade of
syntax errors that point at WGSL and read as a corrupted file rather than a quoting mistake.

It cost two separate debugging sessions in this module. **U10** now asserts that no generator output
contains a backtick at all. When you add WGSL here, quote identifiers with `'single quotes'` in
comments.

---

## 7. Test map

| Test | Pins |
|---|---|
| U1 | cube-face convention, all six faces + corner octants |
| U2 | equirect ↔ direction round-trip |
| U3 | solid angles sum to 4π (catches the midpoint approximation) |
| U4 | SH packing order matches `shCoeff(k)`'s indexing |
| U5 | L2 ringing goes negative raw, clamped in the shipped path |
| U6 / U6b | constant-environment energy (validates A0/A1/A2); rotation consistency |
| U7 | BRDF LUT endpoints + monotonicity direction |
| U8 | every module parses; env claims exactly group-2 bindings 3–6 |
| U9 | the material hook is opt-in and byte-identical when absent |
| U10 | no backtick in any generated WGSL |
| §11 | config validation error messages |

`npm run test:environment` (IBL + probes + sky).

**The sky seam** — `npm run test:sky`:

| Test | Pins |
|---|---|
| U1 | `GradientSky` matches the pre-refactor `skyColor` at 64 directions to 1e-6 — the refactor is numerically inert |
| U2 | the bake kernel and the skybox carry byte-identical `sampleSky` bodies |
| U3 | every shipped source's composed bake kernel and skybox module parses |
| U4 | Preetham zenith luminance rises with turbidity and with `sin(elevation)` |
| U5 | finite, non-negative radiance over 512 directions × 32 solar elevations (−20°..90°) |
| U6 | the `sunRadiance` CPU mirror matches the WGSL's own constants at 32 elevations to 1e-5 |
| U7 | no source declares `PI` or collides with `ENV_MATH_WGSL`; helpers are `sky_`-prefixed |
| U8 | no generated sky WGSL contains a backtick |
| U9 | `EquirectSky` on `keepSourceCube: false` throws, naming the flag |
| U10 | `writeParams` allocates zero bytes across 1,000 calls |
| U11 | source group-2 bindings stay inside the reserved 14–17 range |
| U12 | the shipped `cheapSky` default is 0 — the skybox really does evaluate |
| U13 | every sky header float survives a later partial `setSkyParams` |
| §9 | the build-time error table, verbatim |

**GPU integration** — `npm run test:sky:gpu` (headless Chrome) or open
`/test/environment-gpu/` in a browser:

| Test | Pins |
|---|---|
| T1 | measured sun-disc angular radius matches `sunAngularRadius` within one pixel, at 0.266° — a size the prefiltered cube cannot represent |
| T2 | the skybox (0.5%) and the bake (2%) both reproduce the CPU mirror at 64 directions |
| T3 | radiance is continuous across all 12 cube edges (1%), and edge directions carry the right radiance (2%) |
| T4 | `cheapSky: 1` reproduces the pre-Phase-1 module's image, and `cheapSky: 0` differs |
| T5 | a source swap re-arms the bake and leaves no stale prefilter mip |

docs.title: Film — offline browser rendering (F1–F3)
docs.text:
# Film — offline browser rendering (F1–F3)

**Implementation status, 2026-10-25:**
- **Built:** F1's helpers and engine teardown; F2's managed runner, session, readback, video into
  memory, hashes, measurements and PNG snapshots; F3's storage: video streamed to OPFS or to a file
  the user picked, PNG sequences, Web Locks, and the films an app lists, cleans up and removes.
- **Tested:** the browser G suite passed on an AMD iGPU and an NVIDIA GPU in Chrome
  ([validation](#validation-and-limits)).
- **Later phases:** a worker (F4), application integration validation (outside this repository).

The design and its measurements: `docs/offline-films-browser-design.md` ("Phase F2 results",
"Phase F3 results").

Import from `null-graph/film`. Video encoding needs the optional peer `mediabunny` (tested
with 1.61.3); pure helpers, hashes and snapshots do not. The runner dynamically imports
`null-graph` rather than bundling another copy of the core.

## Managed recording

`recordFilm(options)` creates an isolated engine on your borrowed `GPUDevice`, builds your
workload, calibrates, resets (or rebuilds), warms up, then records. Pause the preview before
calling it and restore the preview in your application's `finally`. Never lend mutable preview
simulation state to the workload. Device loss requires application recovery, not just resume.

Required options:

| Option | Contract |
|---|---|
| `device` | Borrowed GPUDevice; never destroyed by the film. Exports and snapshots serialize per device. |
| `film` | `{ width, height, fps, seconds, warmupSeconds? }`; even dimensions, positive integer fps and a whole number of frames. |
| `createWorkload` | Async factory receiving `{ engine, width, height, signal, defer }`. |

The factory returns `{ dt, step, draw, dispose, reset?, prepare?, info? }`:

- `dt` is a positive fixed timestep. Each frame must contain a whole number of steps.
- `step()` performs bounded work. The runner owns warm-up and filmed step counts.
- `draw(frame)` synchronously returns the engine render sequence; it must not submit or yield.
  `frame` contains `index`, `seconds = index / fps`, `timestampUs`, `durationUs` and `view`.
- `prepare(frame)` may perform bounded derived work before draw.
- `reset()` restores the exact initial state, including placement, without warm-up. If omitted,
  the calibrated workload is disposed and built again on the same film engine.
- `dispose()` releases workload-owned resources and is idempotent. Engine teardown runs afterwards.
- Register partially constructed resources using `defer(release)` immediately after acquisition.
  Those releases run if construction fails; after successful construction `dispose()` owns them.

With W warm-up steps and s steps per frame, frame j shows state W + s × (j + 1), including
frame zero. Calibration changes state, so a complete reset or deterministic rebuild is essential.

Optional runner settings:

| Option | Default / behavior |
|---|---|
| `camera` | Optional `(seconds) => CameraView`; omitted, the workload controls its camera. |
| `source` | `'auto'`: operationally probe offscreen canvas, otherwise readback, before frame zero. |
| `hashes` | `false`; when true forces exact RGBA readback. Explicit canvas + hashes is refused. |
| `output` | Video options; `false` disables video (hash-only or measurement-only). |
| `signal` | AbortSignal; cancellation discards and rejects with AbortError. |
| `partial` | `'discard'`; `'keep-if-finalizable'` may return a finalized partial after a non-cancel failure. |
| `guard` | `{ limitMs?, stopMs? }`, may only lower the 1000/1500 ms defaults. |
| `yieldEveryMs` | 8; real task yields occur after capture. |
| `onProgress` | Phase, frame count, elapsed ms, ms/frame, ETA, encoded bytes and background status. |
| `onReport` | Outcome report once the opened session settles; observer exceptions do not change outcome. |
| `provenance` | Application-supplied metadata for function-valued workloads/cameras. |

Invalid options and session-opening failures can reject before `onReport` is installed. Always
handle the returned promise; do not use `onReport` as the sole error channel.

**Cancelling.** Aborting `signal` rejects with an AbortError and keeps nothing, from any phase:
building, calibrating, resetting, warming up, recording, or a frame held by the encoder.
- **Latency:** in Chrome on both GPUs it was under 7 ms. It runs longer only while your own
  `createWorkload`, `step` or `prepare` is still running: the runner checks between your calls and
  cannot interrupt them.
- **A cancel during the muxer's finalize** joins it, and the film completes. The first terminal
  request wins, and by then the runner has asked to finish. Dispose the result if you no longer want
  it. A cancel that comes before finalizing begins wins.

**Device loss.** A lost device ends the film before its next submission:
`film: GPU device lost at frame <j> (<reason>: <message>); partial file <kept|discarded>.`
- **The encoder can go with the device.** Chrome's hardware encoder lives in its GPU process, so
  when that process crashes, the encoder goes too and never answers again.
- **After a loss** the runner waits up to `LOST_ENCODER_GRACE_MS` (2 s) for the encoder, then gives
  it up. The film ends rather than hanging.
- **Partials are best-effort:** with `partial: 'keep-if-finalizable'`, a partial is kept only if the
  encoder still finalizes it.
- **Recovery is the app's:** request a new adapter and device, rebuild what used the old one (your
  preview included), and film again. A lost device is never resumed.

**Hidden and frozen pages.** Film time comes from the frame number, never the wall clock, so a film
hashes the same whatever happened to the page.
- **Hidden:** a hidden page films at its usual pace (measured: within 5% on both GPUs). Its timers
  fire at most once a second, so a workload's `step()` should not wait on timers: the guard would
  read the wait as a slow operation, and could stop the film.
- **Frozen:** a frozen page (Page Lifecycle's `freeze`) runs no task, and the film waits. An
  operation measured across a freeze is not judged against the guard's limits (they would be timing
  the freeze). `report.guard.unjudged` counts such operations.

## Output, storage and results

Output options are `container`, `codecs`, `bitrate`, `hardwareAcceleration`, `target`, `name` and
`memoryBudgetBytes`.
- **Containers:** `'mp4'` (H.264 alone unless you list more), `'webm'` (VP9, then AV1), or `'png'`,
  a PNG sequence: each frame's exact bytes as a file of its own.
- **Bitrate:** a video's bitrate defaults to `round(width × height × fps × 0.16)`. The asked bitrate
  is not what an encoder delivers: the report gives both (rate control is the design's parked Q9).
- **`hardwareAcceleration`** (1.2.1): WebCodecs' encoder preference, `'no-preference'` (default, the
  browser's choice), `'prefer-software'` or `'prefer-hardware'`. A software encoder honours the
  bitrate at sizes some hardware encoders do not, such as a 4K film. The codec is checked under the
  same preference before frame 0 (`probeFilm` takes it too), so a refusal names it; the report's
  `output.hardwareAcceleration` and `encoderConfig` say what was asked and what was configured. Not
  for a PNG sequence.
- **`name`** is the download name: metadata, never a path.

**Where the file goes (`target`).** It is chosen before frame 0 and never changed during the film; the
report says where it went and why (`report.output.target`, `targetReason`).

| `target` | What happens |
|---|---|
| `'auto'` (default) | OPFS where it is there, has room for the film's predicted bytes, and takes a write. Otherwise memory, within `memoryBudgetBytes`, saying why. Otherwise a refusal giving both reasons: never a silent escalation. |
| `'opfs'` | OPFS, or a refusal: `film: not enough storage in OPFS — <need> MB needed, <avail> MB available.` |
| `'memory'` | A Blob, within `memoryBudgetBytes` (default 256 MiB of encoded payload, not of process memory: spike S1 measured about 3× the payload at peak). |
| `{ file: handle }` | The `FileSystemFileHandle` your app got from `showSaveFilePicker` in a user gesture. The library never opens a picker or asks for permission. |

A PNG sequence goes to OPFS only (`'auto'` or `'opfs'`), and is read back: its frames need exact bytes.

**In OPFS** a film is `null-graph-films/<exportId>/`: its payload (`film.mp4`, or a `frames/` folder of
`frame-000000.png`, …) beside its manifest, `film.json`.
- **While it is written:** the manifest says `writing`, and the film's Web Lock
  (`null-graph-film:<exportId>`) is held. Video writes wait in the browser's swap file, so the payload
  reads empty until committed.
- **When it is committed:** once the muxer has finalized, the library commits the file; only then does
  the manifest say `completed` (or `partial`), with the film's report. mediabunny also closes its
  stream when it cancels and when a finalize fails; neither close commits anything.
- **When it is discarded** (cancelled, failed, out of room): nothing is kept, and the folder is
  removed. The library aborts the file's writable, where closing it would commit a half film (spike
  S1's finding).
- **If the manifest cannot be marked complete**, the film is removed, and the error says so: an
  unmarked film would look abandoned to every later cleanup.
- **Memory:** an MP4 streamed to a file reserves its index at the front for the film's J frames
  (`ftyp moov free mdat`), so it plays as it loads. The page then holds the frames in flight and two
  16 MiB chunks, not the film: through a 60 s 4K film, its JS memory moved by under 2 MiB while the
  file grew to 57.7 MiB (Phase F3 results).
- **A storage check runs before frame 0**, comparing the predicted bytes with OPFS's estimate. It is
  an estimate, not a reservation: a write can still run out of room mid-film, which ends the film with
  `film: OPFS ran out of room at frame <j> (QuotaExceededError: …); free some storage, or film shorter
  or at a lower bitrate.`

**A picked file** is the user's. It is written through its handle and committed when the film is
finalized; a discarded film, one that fails at finalize included, leaves the file as it was (a file the
picker just made stays, empty), and `dispose()` never touches it. A handle the browser refuses at write time is refused in plain words:
`film: the chosen file "<name>" may not be written (NotAllowedError: …); ask for write permission in a
user gesture (handle.requestPermission({ mode: 'readwrite' })) and try again.`

A successful result has `{ status, file, name, codec, target, exportId, sequence, frames, report, dispose }`:

- **`status`** is `'completed'` or `'partial'`. A partial must have finalized, been committed and, in
  OPFS, been marked `partial`; `report.failure` says why it stopped.
- **`file`** is the video: a Blob in memory, or a `File` read from OPFS or the picked file, which holds
  no memory. It is null for a PNG sequence and when the output is off.
- **`target`** is `'memory'`, `'opfs'` or `'file'`. `exportId` names the film's OPFS folder (null
  elsewhere), as `listFilms` names it.
- **`sequence`** is a PNG sequence's frames folder (a `FileSystemDirectoryHandle`) and its file names,
  frame 0 first; null for a video.
- **`dispose()`** removes the film's OPFS folder, after which its `File` reads no more. It does nothing
  for memory (you revoke your own object URLs) or for a picked file. It is idempotent. Keep the film
  until it has been downloaded or shared: a download click is no sign that it is done.
- **Reports** include:
  - where the film went (`output.target`, `targetReason`, `storage`: path, lock, committed, and the
    storage check's numbers);
  - source selection, planned/accepted/encoded frames, encoder config, bytes and the achieved
    bitrate;
  - timings, hashes when requested, state history, GPU errors, a lost device's reason, and
    secondary cleanup failures;
  - the guard's evidence: calibration, fencing, where fencing switched, the worst fenced step and
    draw, and the operations left unjudged.

## Films in OPFS

An app sees the films it has made, in this tab or another, and decides what to remove.

- **`listFilms()`** lists every film, oldest first, and changes nothing. Each entry gives `exportId`,
  `status` (`writing`, `completed`, `partial`, or `unknown` when no manifest was written), `name`,
  `container`, `frames`, `bytes`, `created`, `report`, `getFile()` and `getFrames()`. It also gives
  `live`: a writer holds the film's lock now, in any tab (null where Web Locks are missing).
- **`cleanupFilms()`** removes the incomplete films no writer holds: those whose tab closed, crashed
  or was discarded mid-film. It removes a film only while holding that film's lock, so a film being
  written anywhere is kept, and only if the film's manifest, read again under that lock, still says
  it is incomplete, so a film that completes while cleanup runs is kept too. Completed and partial
  films are kept, even old ones: removing those is the app's call. Without Web Locks a live film cannot be told from an abandoned one, so it removes
  nothing and says why. It never resumes a film. It returns `{ removed, kept }`, each kept film with
  its reason.
- **`removeFilm(exportId)`** removes one film, completed or not. It refuses one being written now:
  `film: the film "<id>" is being written now (its lock is held); stop or cancel that film first.`

Two tabs never collide: every film has a random export id, whatever its name. Nothing is swept
automatically, not even by `probeFilm`.

OPFS is best-effort storage: under storage pressure the browser may evict it, films included.
Whether to ask for persistence (`navigator.storage.persist()`) is the app's decision. The library
never asks, and never promises a film survives eviction, a cleared site or a discarded tab.

## App-driven sessions

`createFilmSession({ film, output?, mediabunny?, signal? })` supplies the frames-in/file-out
piece without creating an engine; its `output` chooses a target as `recordFilm`'s does. Await
`session.add(videoFrame)` for backpressure. Ownership transfers on invocation, including rejected
adds: do not close the frame again. A PNG sequence's frames must be 8-bit RGB(A) VideoFrames at the
film's size (`'RGBA'` keeps alpha; `'RGBX'` writes it opaque).

Stamp frame j with `frameStamp(j, fps)`: timestamp is `round(j × 1e6 / fps)` microseconds,
duration is the next timestamp minus this one. Do not pass seconds to VideoFrame.

- **`finish()`** requires the planned video frames and finalizes.
- **`stop()`** keeps a finalized nonempty partial; `{ keepPartial: false }` discards.
- **`cancel()`** discards and waits for teardown.
  - It cancels the encoder first, so it does not wait for a frame the encoder holds.
  - Frames queued behind that one are closed without being encoded.
- **The first terminal operation wins.** Calls made after finalization has begun join its outcome;
  they do not interrupt an in-progress finalization.
- **`abandon(error)`** is the exception: it stops waiting on an encoder that will not answer, even
  inside a `finish()` under way. The wait in flight, and every one after it, fails with `error`, and
  the session ends `failed`. `recordFilm` calls it after a device loss; call it yourself if your own
  loop finds its encoder gone. What mediabunny still holds of the dead encoder is left to the
  garbage collector.
- **A premature `finish()` refusal** leaves the session open to add more frames or stop/cancel.

Use `try/finally` to cancel an unfinished session if your app-driven loop fails.

## Readback, snapshots and pure helpers

`FrameReadback(device, texture, width, height)` reads rgba8unorm textures with 256-byte GPU
row padding removed. `grab(index)` queues a copy; keep at most two pending grabs. Await
`take(out?)` or `takeVideoFrame(timestampUs, durationUs)`. The latter uses RGBX, ignoring alpha
for opaque video. `take()` without an output buffer reuses its storage: copy bytes if retaining
them across calls. Call `destroy()` in `finally`.

`snapshot({ device, createWorkload, width, height, seconds?, view?, signal? })` draws exactly
once, steps nothing, and returns `{ png, rgba, width, height, limitations }`. Odd PNG dimensions
are allowed. `seconds` is a draw time, not an instruction to advance simulation state.

Pure helpers include `planFilm`, `frameStamp`, `readCamera`, `cameraPath`, `fitAspect`,
`containAspect`, `bitrateFor`, `predictBytes`, `encodePNG`, `crc32` and `sha256` (Web Crypto).
`probeFilm` is cheap capability evidence, not an export guarantee: operational capture,
encoding, allocation and storage can still fail at runtime.
- **What it does by default:** it writes nothing.
- **With `operational: true`** it writes a byte to OPFS under a folder of its own
  (`null-graph-films/.probe-<uuid>/`), holding that folder's lock as every writer does, and removes it
  again, so `targets.opfs.writable` says whether OPFS takes a write here.
- **`targets.locks`** says whether Web Locks exist, without which `cleanupFilms` cannot tell
  live films from abandoned ones.

## Validation and limits

After `npm run build:lib`:
- **`npm run test:film`** (114 tests) runs the whole runner headless, on stand-ins for the device,
  WebCodecs, mediabunny, OPFS and Web Locks. It includes garbage-collection checks that no film keeps
  its engine alive, and no result its session.
- **`npm run test:core`.**
- **`node test/film-browser-smoke.mjs`** films with real Node/Dawn readback, reset, hashes and
  snapshots, on the adapter that `NG_DAWN_FLAGS=adapter=AMD` or `adapter=NVIDIA` selects.
- **`npm run test:film:browser`** is the G suite. It runs `recordFilm` in Chrome on each GPU
  (`--gpu amd,nvidia`, `--only <cases>`, `--long`, `--headed`), loading `dist/film.js` through an
  import map, and reads every film back with ffprobe and ffmpeg. It needs both on `PATH`. Its 17
  cases check:
  - **G1:** the same film twice hashes the same, and nothing is left on the device;
  - **G2:** exact readback bytes, and decoded colours per codec and range; **G2-png:** a PNG
    sequence's frames, byte for byte;
  - **G3:** J frames, timestamps on their ticks, key frames, the MP4 layout for each target, and
    frame k showing k;
  - **G4:** Kerr at 4K streamed to OPFS, the page's JS memory flat while the file grows (G4-long, a
    60 s film, runs with `--long`);
  - **G5:** the guard; **G5-storage:** a discarded film leaves nothing in OPFS;
  - **G6:** canvas against readback;
  - **G7:** two tabs: a live writer's film is kept, an orphan is cleaned up;
  - **G8:** refused and picked files, a full quota, encoder and finalize failures, lost devices;
  - **G9:** cancellation, the main thread and the preview, hidden and frozen pages, `destroy()`,
    and a crashed GPU process.

  Every case fails if it leaves anything in OPFS. On 2026-10-25 it passed 422 checks on each GPU,
  and G4-long its 15.

**Limits:**
- **The guard measures time, not the GPU.** It measures queue-completion wall time, not GPU
  timestamps, and cannot interrupt a submission already in flight.
- **The first submission is unqualified:** it compiles the pipelines, and nothing qualifies it as
  safe.
- **The guard re-measures an isolated stall once (Q10).** When a fenced operation passes the stop
  but its calibrated operation was under a quarter of the stop, the runner measures the next fenced
  operation before stopping, so a single desktop stall does not end the film.
- **Untested:** Firefox and Safari, a real TDR, and a real `showSaveFilePicker` handle (the G suite
  writes through an OPFS file's handle, which has the same interface).
