docs.text:
# Geometry API Usage

The `null-graph/geometry` module is the math and primitive toolbox. It generates vertex/index data
for common shapes, lets you define custom vertex layouts on the fly, and packs everything into
WebGPU-ready buffers. Because NullGraph has no scene graph, geometry is just raw typed-array data
plus a layout description — no nodes, no hierarchy.

```ts
import {
    Primitives, VertexLayout, StandardLayout, CompleteLayout, PositionOnlyLayout,
    Geometry, GeometryBuilder,
} from 'null-graph/geometry';
```

---

## Vertex layouts

A `VertexLayout` describes the interleaved attributes in a vertex buffer and computes the stride
for you. Three presets cover most cases:

| Preset | Attributes | Stride (floats) |
|---|---|---|
| `PositionOnlyLayout` | Position | 3 |
| `StandardLayout` | Position, Normal, UV | 8 |
| `CompleteLayout` | Position, Normal, UV, Color | 11 |

```ts
// Custom layout
const layout = new VertexLayout([
    VertexAttribute.Position,
    VertexAttribute.Normal,
    VertexAttribute.UV,
]);

layout.strideFloats;                // number of floats per vertex
layout.getWebGPUDescriptor();       // GPUVertexBufferLayout[] for createBatch({ vertexLayouts })
```

## Primitives

`Primitives` is a static factory that returns a `Geometry` for each shape. Every method takes a
layout so the output matches the vertex format your shader expects.

```ts
const cube         = Primitives.createCube(StandardLayout, 2, 2, 2);             // width, height, depth
const plane        = Primitives.createPlane(StandardLayout, 10, 10);             // width, height
const pyramid      = Primitives.createPyramid(StandardLayout, 2, 2, 2);          // width, height, depth
const sphere       = Primitives.createSphere(StandardLayout, 30, 10, 10);        // radius, widthSegments, heightSegments
const torus        = Primitives.createTorus(StandardLayout, 20, 10, 20, 30);     // radius, tubeRadius, radialSegments, tubularSegments
const octahedron   = Primitives.createOctahedron(StandardLayout, 2, 2, 2);       // width, height, depth
const icosahedron  = Primitives.createIcosahedron(StandardLayout, 1);            // radius
const tetrahedron  = Primitives.createTetrahedron(StandardLayout, 1);            // radius
const dodecahedron = Primitives.createDodecahedron(StandardLayout, 1);           // radius
const cylinder     = Primitives.createCylinder(StandardLayout, 5, 5, 10, 16, 1); // radiusTop, radiusBottom, height, radSeg, heightSeg
const cone         = Primitives.createCone(StandardLayout, 5, 10, 16, 1);        // radius, height, radSeg, heightSeg
const capsule      = Primitives.createCapsule(StandardLayout, 5, 10, 8, 16);     // radius, length, capSeg, radSeg
const ring         = Primitives.createRing(StandardLayout, 5, 10, 32);           // innerRadius, outerRadius, thetaSeg
```

Available factories: `createCube`, `createPlane`, `createPyramid`, `createOctahedron`, 
`createIcosahedron`, `createTetrahedron`, `createDodecahedron`, `createSphere`, 
`createTorus`, `createCylinder`, `createCone`, `createCapsule`, `createRing`.

### Which way each shape faces

Every shape is centred on the origin, in its own axes (checked in 1.2.1's sources):

- **`createPlane` stands upright**: a quad in **XY at z = 0**, facing **+Z**, with a back face toward −Z so it shows
  from behind too (as three.js's plane does). It is not a floor. To lay it flat, turn it −90° about X; its `height`
  then runs along Z.
- **`createRing`** lies in XY too, facing ±Z. **`createTorus`** lies flat in **XZ**, around the Y axis.
- **`createCylinder`, `createCone`, `createCapsule` and `createPyramid`** stand along **Y**, the cone's tip and the
  pyramid's apex up.
- `createCube`, `createPyramid` and `createOctahedron` take width, height and depth along X, Y and Z.
- Only the factories that take segment counts have them. The cube, plane, pyramid, octahedron and the three
  polyhedra are a fixed set of faces.

The stock materials' vertex shaders scale each vertex by its instance's scale, then rotate it, then move it
([Materials](./materials.md#things-to-know)). So an instance's scale is in the shape's own axes. A plane laid flat by a
−90° turn about X needs the scale `(width, depth, 1)`, not `(width, 1, depth)`.

## `Geometry`

A `Geometry` holds the CPU-side `vertices` (`Float32Array`) and `indices` (`Uint16Array` or
`Uint32Array`) plus the layout, and uploads them to GPU buffers.

```ts
const geom = Primitives.createCube(StandardLayout, 2, 2, 2);
geom.upload(engine); // creates geom.vertexBuffer and geom.indexBuffer

engine.setBatchGeometry(
    batch,
    geom.vertexBuffer!,
    geom.indexBuffer!,
    geom.indices.length,
);

// Free VRAM when done
geom.destroy();
```

## `GeometryBuilder`

For procedural meshes, `GeometryBuilder` accumulates vertices and indices into growable arrays and
bakes them into flat typed arrays — useful for voxel chunks, marching cubes, extruded paths, or any
mesh you generate at runtime. You add vertices (getting back an index) and stitch them into triangles.

### API

```ts
const builder = new GeometryBuilder(StandardLayout);

// addVertex(data) appends one vertex and returns its index
const i0 = builder.addVertex({ position: [-1, -1, 0], normal: [0, 0, 1], uv: [0, 0] });
const i1 = builder.addVertex({ position: [ 1, -1, 0], normal: [0, 0, 1], uv: [1, 0] });
const i2 = builder.addVertex({ position: [ 1,  1, 0], normal: [0, 0, 1], uv: [1, 1] });
const i3 = builder.addVertex({ position: [-1,  1, 0], normal: [0, 0, 1], uv: [0, 1] });

// addTriangle(a, b, c) references vertices by the indices returned above
builder.addTriangle(i0, i1, i2);
builder.addTriangle(i0, i2, i3);

// build() bakes the accumulated data into typed arrays
const baked = builder.build();
// baked = { v: Float32Array, i: Uint16Array, vertexBuffer, indexBuffer, layout }
// (`v`/`vertexBuffer` and `i`/`indexBuffer` are aliases of the same data)
```

`VertexData` accepted by `addVertex`:

```ts
interface VertexData {
    position: [number, number, number];  // required
    normal?:  [number, number, number];  // defaults to [0, 1, 0] if omitted
    uv?:      [number, number];
    color?:   [number, number, number, number];
}
```

### Uploading a built mesh

`build()` returns **plain typed arrays**, not a `Geometry`. Wrap them in a `Geometry` to reuse its
`upload()`/`destroy()` lifecycle:

```ts
const baked = builder.build();
const geom = new Geometry(baked.layout, baked.v, baked.i);
geom.upload(engine);

engine.setBatchGeometry(batch, geom.vertexBuffer!, geom.indexBuffer!, geom.indices.length);
```

Or create the GPU buffers directly if you don't need the `Geometry` wrapper:

```ts
const vertexBuffer = engine.bufferManager.createVertexBuffer(baked.v);
const indexBuffer  = engine.bufferManager.createIndexBuffer(baked.i);
engine.setBatchGeometry(batch, vertexBuffer, indexBuffer, baked.i.length);
```

### Things to know

- **The builder emits `Position (3) + Normal (3) + UV (2)` — i.e. the `StandardLayout` (8 floats).**
  Always pass `uv` when targeting `StandardLayout`; omitting it writes only 6 floats for that vertex
  and desyncs the whole vertex stride.
- **`color` is accepted by `VertexData` but not written** by `addVertex`, so the builder does not
  currently produce `CompleteLayout` geometry. Use `Primitives`/manual `Float32Array`s for colored
  vertices, or push into `builder.vertices` yourself.
- **Indices are `Uint16Array`**, capping a single builder at 65,536 vertices. Split large meshes into
  multiple builders/batches (or write `Uint32Array` indices manually).
- `builder.vertices` and `builder.indices` are plain `number[]` you can also read or mutate directly
  before calling `build()`.

> For very large, streaming worlds see `DynamicGeometryManager` and `MegaBufferBuilder` (also
> exported from this module), which pack many meshes into shared mega-buffers to minimize buffer
> churn and state changes.

---

## `MeshletBuilder` (v1.0.5)

Partitions each mesh into **meshlets** — small clusters of ≤64 vertices / ≤124 triangles, each
carrying a bounding sphere and a backface normal cone — and packs the result into flat typed arrays
ready to upload as GPU storage buffers. Meshlets are the unit of sub-object culling consumed by the
companion [`VisibilitySystem`](../visibility-design.md). This is a **build-time** module: it never
touches a `GPUDevice`, so it runs in a Web Worker or a Node bake script and costs nothing per frame.
See [`geometry-meshlets-design.md`](../geometry-meshlets-design.md) for the full contract.

`MeshletBuilder` is layered **on top of** `MegabufferBuilder`: meshlet vertex references are global
indices into the shared mega vertex pool, so one vertex allocation backs both the instance tier and
the meshlet tier (design doc §2.1).

```ts
import { MegabufferBuilder, MeshletBuilder } from 'null-graph/geometry';

const mega = new MegabufferBuilder(8);                 // 8 floats/vertex: pos(3) normal(3) uv(2)
const builder = new MeshletBuilder(mega, {
    positionOffsetFloats: 0,
    maxVertices: 64,        // clamp 1..255 (local indices are 8-bit)
    maxTriangles: 124,      // clamp 1..124 (the companion draw expansion)
});

// one LOD:
const rock = builder.addMesh('rock', { vertices: rockVerts, indices: rockIndices });

// or an explicit LOD chain (pre-decimated index arrays you supply):
builder.addMesh('tree', {
    vertices: treeVerts,
    lods: [
        { indices: treeLOD0, error: 0.0  },   // world-space geometric error vs LOD0, in mesh units
        { indices: treeLOD1, error: 0.05 },
        { indices: treeLOD2, error: 0.20 },
    ],
});

const pack = builder.build();
```

`addMesh` returns `{ meshIndex, name }`; `meshIndex` is what an instance stores to reference the
mesh. `build()` returns a `MeshletPack`:

| Field | Type | Upload usage | Contents |
|---|---|---|---|
| `megaVertices` | `Float32Array` | `VERTEX \| STORAGE` | the shared mega vertex pool |
| `meshlets` | `ArrayBuffer` (64 B stride) | `STORAGE` | `boundsCenter`, `coneApex`, `coneAxis`, `{vertexOffset, triangleOffset, vertexCount, triangleCount}` |
| `meshletVertices` | `Uint32Array` | `STORAGE` | flat global vertex indices |
| `meshletTriangles` | `Uint32Array` | `STORAGE` | 3 × 8-bit local indices packed per u32 |
| `meshLODs` | `Float32Array` (16 B stride) | `STORAGE` | `[meshletOffset, meshletCount, error, 0]` per LOD |
| `meshTable` | `Uint32Array` (16 B stride) | `STORAGE` | `[lodOffset, lodCount, 0, 0]` per mesh |
| `report` | `MeshletReport` | — | counts, `vertexReuse` (want < 1.2), `avgVerticesPerMeshlet` (want > 55), `bytes` |

Uploading is the app's job (one `BufferManager.createBuffer` call each), because usage flags differ
per buffer and the builder must not depend on a live device. `build()` also finalizes the shared
`mega`, so `mega.getOffset(name)` stays valid afterward for the meshlet-free instance tier.

Things to know:

- **Deterministic** — the same mesh in produces byte-identical buffers out (property P5), so builds
  are diffable.
- **`meshletTriangles.length` equals the input triangle count exactly** — meshletization partitions
  triangles, never duplicates them.
- Out-of-range indices, non-÷3 index arrays, degenerate LODs, duplicate names, and cap overflows
  (`maxTriangles > 124`, `maxVertices > 255`) all **throw at build time** naming the offending mesh.

docs.title: Inference — networks from files, and ONNX Runtime
docs.text:
# Inference — networks from files, and ONNX Runtime

Import from `null-graph/inference`. The entry is for running, in an app, a network that was
trained elsewhere. It does that in two ways:

- **`mlpFromOnnx`** reads a small dense network from the bytes of an `.onnx` file, for
  [`MlpBrain`](./agents.md#network-brains-mlpbrain) to run. The file is read once, on the CPU, by
  this library, and the network then runs on the GPU as `MlpBrain`'s think stage, like any other.
  No ONNX Runtime, and no dependency. Design:
  [`agents-onnx-reader-design.md`](../agents-onnx-reader-design.md).
- **`OrtRuntime`, `OrtModel` and `OrtBrain`** run a model through ONNX Runtime Web's WebGPU
  provider, over GPU buffers ([below](#onnx-runtime)). `OrtBrain` makes such a model the brain of
  one or more species. ONNX Runtime is the app's dependency: an optional peer of this package,
  which the app installs and imports. Design: [`agents-ort-design.md`](../agents-ort-design.md).

**Use `mlpFromOnnx` and `MlpBrain` when the network fits them.** ONNX Runtime costs 3× to 10× the
built-in kernel's GPU time for the same network, a 6.4 MB download, and up to 1.6 s to start
([cost](#what-onnx-runtime-costs)). It is for the networks `MlpBrain` cannot run: deeper or wider,
or with other operators.

**Both, side by side:** the test site's Herd & Wolves demo ([nullgraph.dev](https://nullgraph.dev/),
`/dashboard/agents/herd-wolves-gpu`) runs one trained network as `MlpBrain` and through ONNX
Runtime (`OrtBrain`), switched live per species, with each one's GPU time on screen. Before it
runs an `.onnx` file, it reads the file with `mlpFromOnnx` and checks that it holds the
`.mlp.json`'s weights, bit for bit.

## Load a network

```ts
import type { NullGraph } from 'null-graph';
import { MlpBrain, type AgentSystem } from 'null-graph/agents';
import { mlpFromOnnx, type OnnxExternalData } from 'null-graph/inference';

/**
 * Puts the dense network of an .onnx file on one species. The caller owns the returned brain.
 * `externalData` holds the second file PyTorch writes beside the .onnx file by default.
 */
export function useOnnxNetwork(engine: NullGraph, agents: AgentSystem, bytes: ArrayBuffer | Uint8Array, species: string,
    externalData: OnnxExternalData[] = []) {
    const { network, metadata } = mlpFromOnnx(bytes, { externalData });   // throws, naming the node, when it is not a dense network
    // A file written by this repository's exporter carries the names it was trained with. Equal
    // widths cannot show that an input means what the network expects; equal names do.
    const { obsNames, actNames } = agents.definition;
    for (const [key, names] of [['obsNames', obsNames], ['actNames', actNames]] as const) {
        if (metadata[key] !== undefined && JSON.parse(metadata[key]).join() !== names.join()) {
            throw new Error(`The file was trained on other ${key === 'obsNames' ? 'observations' : 'actions'} than "${species}" has.`);
        }
    }
    const brain = new MlpBrain(engine, network);         // refuses more layers, or wider ones, than it runs
    try {
        agents.setBrain(brain, { species });             // refuses widths that are not the definition's
    } catch (error) {
        brain.destroy();
        throw error;
    }
    return brain;
}
```

Call it with the file's bytes, for example
`useOnnxNetwork(engine, agents, await (await fetch('prey.onnx')).arrayBuffer(), 'prey')`. Destroy
the system, or give the species another brain, before destroying the returned brain.

- **`mlpFromOnnx(bytes, { externalData })`** takes a `Uint8Array` or an `ArrayBuffer`, and, when
  the exporter stored weights in a second file, that file: `externalData: [{ path, data }]`, with
  `path` as the `.onnx` file names it (`policy.onnx.data`) and `data` its bytes. It is the list
  ONNX Runtime takes. It returns `{ network, input, output, metadata }`:
  - `network` is an `MlpNetwork`. It also feeds `MlpBrain.bySpecies`, `brain.setWeights` and
    `mlpForward`.
  - `input` and `output` are the graph's names for its input and its output.
  - `metadata` is what the file says about itself, as text; it is empty for most files.
- **The weights come back bit for bit,** in arrays of their own. The bytes may be dropped after
  the call.
- **A file that is not a dense network is refused** with an error that names the node or the
  tensor and says what to do ([below](#when-a-file-is-refused)). Nothing is approximated.
- **`MlpBrain`'s limits are `MlpBrain`'s.** The reader takes a network of any depth and width;
  `new MlpBrain` refuses more than 4 layers, an input wider than 128, a hidden layer wider than
  64, an output wider than 16, and a weight that is not finite.

## What a file must hold

- **One chain of dense layers** from one input to one output. A layer is `Gemm`, or `MatMul` with
  an optional `Add` for the bias, followed by at most one of `Relu`, `Tanh`, `Sigmoid`.
- **Weights and biases as float32,** stored in the file, or in a second file given as
  `externalData`. A second file is found by its name exactly as the `.onnx` file writes it; the
  reader opens and fetches nothing itself.
- **These are passed over, because they change no value:** a `Cast` to float32 or a `Flatten`
  before the first layer, a `Reshape` after the last, and an `Identity` on a layer's weights or
  bias. scikit-learn and PyTorch's older exporter write them.
- **Not read:** convolutions, recurrent layers, normalization layers, residual connections, and
  other activations (`LeakyRelu`, `Elu`, `Gelu`, `Clip`, `Softmax`); a graph with several inputs
  or outputs; float64 or float16 weights; weights in a second file that is not given.

## Exporting from PyTorch

```python
import torch
from torch import nn

policy = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(24, 64), nn.Tanh(), nn.Linear(64, 64), nn.Tanh(), nn.Linear(64, 2), nn.Tanh()).eval()
example = torch.zeros(1, 24)                       # one row of observations: [1, obsDim]
torch.onnx.export(policy, (example,), "policy.onnx", external_data=False)
```

- **One file with `external_data=False`, or two files without it.** Without the argument,
  PyTorch stores every weight tensor larger than 256 bytes in a second file, `policy.onnx.data`,
  and `policy.onnx` alone holds the graph and the small tensors. Measured with PyTorch 2.14.1: this
  24→64→64→2 network is one file of 30,794 B with the argument, and two files of 7,927 B and
  23,040 B without it. To read two files, fetch both and pass the second:
  `mlpFromOnnx(bytes, { externalData: [{ path: 'policy.onnx.data', data }] })`. Given only the
  first, the reader refuses it and names both ways out.
- **Export the policy alone.** A model that also estimates a value has two outputs, and the
  reader takes one. Export the part that maps observations to actions: for a model with a `pi`
  and a `vf` part, `torch.onnx.export(model.pi, (example,), "policy.onnx", external_data=False)`.
- **Keep it float32.** A model converted with `.double()` is refused.
- **The example's batch size does not matter.** The reader takes its shapes from the weights.
- **Your file paths are in the file.** PyTorch's default exporter writes a stack trace into every
  node, with the paths of your script and of your Python installation. The reader skips them.
  Before publishing a model, remove them:

  ```python
  import onnx

  model = onnx.load("policy.onnx")
  for node in model.graph.node:
      del node.metadata_props[:]
  onnx.save(model, "policy.onnx")
  ```

- **The older exporter** (`dynamo=False`) writes one file with no paths in it, and is read as
  well.

## Exporting from scikit-learn

```python
import numpy
from skl2onnx import to_onnx

with open("policy.onnx", "wb") as file:
    file.write(to_onnx(regressor, X[:1].astype(numpy.float32)).SerializeToString())
```

- **An `MLPRegressor` is read,** with any of its activations (`identity`, `logistic`, `tanh`,
  `relu`) and any number of outputs.
- **An `MLPClassifier` is not:** its file ends in operators that pick a class, and is refused.

## From this repository's trainer

`npm run agents:export` writes each trained Herd & Wolves network as a 41 KB `.onnx` file, with
the observation and action names it was trained with in the file's metadata
([`tools/agents/README.md`](../../tools/agents/README.md)). `mlpFromOnnx` reads such a file back
to the committed network bit for bit, and the example above checks its names.

## When a file is refused

Every refusal is an `Error` whose message starts with `mlpFromOnnx:`. It is thrown when the file is
loaded, never during a frame. The common ones:

| The message says | What to do |
|---|---|
| `initializer "…" is stored outside the file, in "….onnx.data"; pass that file, …` | Pass the second file as `externalData`, with the path the message names. Or export again with the weights inside the file; in PyTorch: `external_data=False` |
| `initializer "…" reads … B at offset … of "…", which holds … B` | The second file given is not the one the `.onnx` file was written with, or it is cut short |
| `the graph has 1 inputs and 2 outputs` | Export the policy alone, not the policy with its value estimate |
| `node "…" is <Op>; supported: Gemm, MatMul, Add, Relu, Tanh, Sigmoid` | The model is not a plain dense network, or uses an activation `MlpBrain` does not have. Retrain with `tanh`, `relu` or `sigmoid`, or run the model through [ONNX Runtime](#onnx-runtime) |
| `initializer "…" has data type 11; only float32 (1) is read` | Convert the model to float32 before exporting |
| `the file's bytes are not protobuf; it is not ONNX` | The bytes are something else: often a web page returned for a wrong address. Check the response before reading it |
| `the file ends inside a field; it is cut short or is not ONNX` | The download was cut short |
| `MlpBrain: expected 1–4 affine layers` or `MlpBrain: layer … must be 1–64` (from `new MlpBrain`) | The network is deeper or wider than the built-in kernel runs |
| `AgentSystem: the brain maps 5→3; the layout is 24→2` (from `setBrain`) | The network was trained for other observations or actions than this definition has |

## What nothing checks

- **What each input means.** A file from another tool carries no names. The reader cannot tell
  whether the network's third input is this definition's third observation. Train on the
  observations in `definition.obsNames`, in that order.
- **Scaling.** If the network was trained on normalized observations, the app must normalize them
  the same way; no file says so.
- **Behaviour.** The reader preserves the weights. `MlpBrain` then agrees with the CPU reference
  `mlpForward` within `1e-5 + 1e-5·|cpu|` for weights of unit scale
  ([agents.md](./agents.md#network-brains-mlpbrain)).

## What the reader costs

- **Size:** `mlpFromOnnx` is 2.5 KB min+gzip. An app that does not import it carries none of it.
- **Time:** reading a 41 KB file takes about 2 ms.
- **Safety with files you did not make:** a damaged or hostile file is refused or read; it cannot
  hang the reader, and the reader never holds more than a few times the file's size.

## ONNX Runtime

`OrtRuntime` starts ONNX Runtime Web's WebGPU provider and keeps its device. `OrtModel` is one
model on it, bound once to GPU buffers. `OrtBrain` runs a model as an agents brain. The app
installs `onnxruntime-web` (1.29 is tested) and passes its namespace; this package never imports
or bundles it.

```ts
import * as ort from 'onnxruntime-web/webgpu';
import { NullGraph } from 'null-graph';
import type { AgentSystem } from 'null-graph/agents';
import { OrtBrain, OrtRuntime } from 'null-graph/inference';

/** ONNX Runtime first: it makes the device, and the engine adopts it. */
export async function startWithOrt(canvas: HTMLCanvasElement) {
    const runtime = await OrtRuntime.create(ort);                        // loads the WASM, makes the device: 0.5–0.7 s
    const engine = new NullGraph();
    const init = await engine.init(canvas, { device: runtime.device });   // adopts it, and never destroys it
    if (!init.success) {
        await runtime.destroy();
        throw new Error(init.error);
    }
    return { runtime, engine };
}

/**
 * Gives `species` the model in `bytes`, run by ONNX Runtime. Its pass is compiled before the
 * switch, so that the switch itself compiles nothing. The caller owns the model and the brain.
 */
export async function useOrtBrain(runtime: OrtRuntime, agents: AgentSystem, bytes: Uint8Array, species: string) {
    const model = await runtime.load(bytes);        // one session: the WebGPU provider, outputs kept on the GPU
    let brain: OrtBrain | undefined;
    try {
        brain = new OrtBrain(model);                // refuses a model that does not map [N, obsDim] to [N, actDim] float32
        await agents.prepareBrain(brain);           // binds the model to the system's buffers; compiles off the frame
        agents.setBrain(brain, { species });        // compiles nothing
        return { model, brain };
    } catch (error) {
        brain?.destroy();
        await model.destroy();
        throw error;
    }
}
```

The frame does not change: `agents.advance(seconds)` also starts a run of the model when none is in
flight. To tear down, stop the frames, then destroy the system, each brain, each model
(`await model.destroy()`), and last the runtime (`await runtime.destroy()`): the device goes with
it, and the engine must not render after.

### The device

- **ONNX Runtime 1.29 runs only on a device it made.** Given the app's device, its sessions are
  created and every run fails, and after a few it can stop answering. So the engine is created
  after the runtime, on `runtime.device`. An app that makes its engine first must make it again
  to use ONNX Runtime.
- **`OrtRuntime.create(ort, { adapter? })`** starts the provider, on the given adapter or one
  ONNX Runtime asks for, and keeps one tiny session of its own for its whole life. ONNX Runtime
  destroys its device with its last session; this one keeps it alive while models come and go.
- **`await runtime.destroy()`** releases every model still loaded, then that session, and with it
  the device.

### Models

- **`await runtime.load(bytes, { capture?, externalData? })`** creates one session. The runtime
  sets its options, and the app cannot change them: the WebGPU provider, outputs kept on the GPU,
  and [graph capture](#graph-capture) only with `capture: true`. `externalData` is ONNX Runtime's
  own option, passed as it is: the same list `mlpFromOnnx` takes, where `data` may also be a URL
  that ONNX Runtime fetches.
- **`model.inputs` and `model.outputs`** list each tensor's `name`, `type` and `dims`: a number,
  or a string for a free axis.
- **`model.bind({ inputs: { name: { buffer, dims } }, outputs: { … } })`, once.** Every input and
  every output gets a GPU buffer: float32, of the model's rank, its fixed axes as the model says,
  and each free axis the same size wherever its name appears. Each buffer needs `STORAGE` usage,
  and its values' bytes rounded up to 16: ONNX Runtime reads and writes 16 B at a time, and on
  NVIDIA a write that ends past a buffer is lost without an error. A second `bind` is refused;
  load the model again for other buffers.
- **`await model.run()`** runs the session over the bound buffers. It resolves once ONNX Runtime
  has queued its GPU work; work submitted after it sees the results. One run of a model at a time.
- **`await model.destroy()`** releases the session, in line: after a run in flight.
- **One call into ONNX Runtime at a time.** ONNX Runtime 1.29 fails two calls in flight across its
  sessions: a session created while another is being created, or a load or a run while another
  model runs, which breaks its memory. So every load, run and release of a runtime's models waits
  in line, in the order made. A call starts at once when none is in line, so one model alone waits
  for nothing, and a call that fails does not hold the line. Two models' runs take turns, and
  `destroy()` can wait for another model's run. Calls an app makes on ONNX Runtime itself are not
  in this line, and neither are a second runtime's: use one runtime.
- **Not supported:** tensor types other than float32 (int64 token inputs, float16, quantized
  models), inputs or outputs on the CPU, and ONNX Runtime's older JavaScript provider (its `all`
  bundle, which ignores a device and cannot load under Node): import `onnxruntime-web/webgpu`.

### OrtBrain

`new OrtBrain(model, { input?, output? })` makes a model the brain of the species `setBrain` gives
it. The names default to the model's only input and only output; a model with several needs them
named.

- **Its shape:** the input `[N, obsDim]` and the output `[N, actDim]`, float32. `N` is a free axis,
  or fixed at the system's `capacity`. PyTorch fixes it at the example's batch size unless told
  otherwise: export with `dynamic_shapes`, or `dynamic_axes={'obs': {0: 'N'}}` with the older
  exporter.
- **How it runs:** each run reads every agent's observations and writes a results buffer of the
  brain's own; its think pass copies each agent's row into the actions, for its species' agents
  that think in that step. Its runs never write the actions themselves.
- **Interactive frames act on the actions of the frame before.** `advance()` starts a run when
  the brain has none in flight and `thinkEvery` steps have passed since its last one started,
  never in a frame without a step. The run reads the observations of that frame and lands before
  the next frame's work. Measured over 300 frames: every frame one frame old under Node, and 299
  of 300 in Chrome. When frames come faster than runs, a run can span several frames (up to 7 in
  Chrome), and the latest run wins.
- **`await agents.step()` is exact:** it senses, waits for the run, then acts. Prey on
  `OrtBrain` act within 1.1e-5 of the same network on `MlpBrain` in the same step, and two runs
  of 120 steps give the same bytes.
- **`thinkEvery` is the rate of runs.** At the default step of 1/60 s, `thinkEvery: 2` runs the
  model 30 times a second, at half the GPU cost ([cost](#what-onnx-runtime-costs)).
- **A brain is bound to one system's buffers,** at its first `setBrain` or `prepareBrain`. Each
  time `setBrain` attaches it, it copies the actions agents have into its results, so a species
  keeps acting as it did until the brain's first run lands (0.14 to 0.46 s for a model's first
  run, which compiles ONNX Runtime's pipelines).
- **A run that fails** is thrown by the next `advance()` or `step()`, once:
  `AgentSystem: the brain of species "prey" failed in a run: <ONNX Runtime's message>. Give the
  species another brain with setBrain().` No run of that brain starts after it, and its species
  keeps its last actions.
- **Prepare it:** `await agents.prepareBrain(brain)` binds the brain and compiles its pass
  ([agents.md](./agents.md#switching-brains-without-a-hitch)), as the example does.
- **A newborn agent** acts for one frame on its slot's last results, before a run has seen it.
- **Mixing:** `OrtBrain` serves its species, and `RuleBrain` or `MlpBrain` the others, in one
  system.
- **Teardown:** destroy the system, or give the brain's species another brain, before
  `brain.destroy()`. The brain releases its results buffer after a run in flight; the model stays
  the app's.

### Graph capture

ONNX Runtime can record a session's GPU work on its first run and replay it after. It costs the
same GPU time and saves main-thread time: 0.20–0.28 ms per run against 0.57–0.69 ms under Node,
and 0.06–0.09 ms against 0.74–0.83 ms in Chrome. **It is off unless `capture: true`,** because of
two faults of ONNX Runtime found here:

- **A captured model can fail from its second run,** with `Cannot set properties of undefined
  (setting 'Symbol(gpuBufferMetadata)')`, sometimes for every run after. Whether it fails depends
  on what ONNX Runtime did between the model's first two runs, such as loading or releasing
  another model, and on the host; on 1.30.0 the smallest case failed with nothing in between.
- **Memory grows with every captured run,** and is never given back while the page lives: 12 MB
  per million runs.

Turn capture on only for a model you measured it on, in the sequence your app runs.
`npm run spike:ort-issues` in this repository shows both faults.

### When a model is refused

Every refusal is thrown when the model is loaded, bound, or given to a system, never during a
frame. The message starts with the class that refused it.

| The message says | What to do |
|---|---|
| `OrtRuntime: that is not onnxruntime-web …` | Pass the namespace of `import * as ort from 'onnxruntime-web/webgpu'` |
| `OrtRuntime: ONNX Runtime could not start its WebGPU provider: …` | The browser or the host has no WebGPU, or ONNX Runtime could not reach its WASM files |
| `OrtRuntime: ONNX Runtime could not load the model: …` | ONNX Runtime's own reason follows; for weights in a second file, pass `externalData` |
| `OrtModel: input "…" is int64; only float32 tensors can be bound.` | The model takes another type: not supported |
| `OrtModel: output "…" is [N,2]; it was given [1000,3].` | The buffer's shape is not the model's |
| `OrtModel: "…" needs 8000 B with STORAGE usage: its values, rounded up to 16 B, …` | Make the buffer that large, with `GPUBufferUsage.STORAGE` |
| `OrtModel: bound already; buffers are fixed for life, …` | Load the model again for other buffers |
| `OrtModel: run() while a run is in flight; await it first.` | One run at a time |
| `OrtBrain: the model has 2 inputs ("obs", "mask"); name the observations with { input: '<name>' }.` | Name the input or the output that `OrtBrain` should use |
| `OrtBrain: input "…" is [N,24] float16; expected [N, obsDim] float32.` | The model takes another type, or its input or output is not a matrix of one row per agent |
| `AgentSystem: the brain maps 32→2; the layout is 24→2.` (from `setBrain`) | The model was trained for other observations or actions than this definition has |
| `OrtBrain: input "…" is [1,24]: its first axis is fixed at 1, and the system has 4096 agents. …` | Export with a free first axis, as the message says |
| `OrtBrain: this system's engine has another device. …` | Init the engine with `{ device: runtime.device }` |
| `OrtBrain: bound to another system's buffers; …` | One brain serves one system; load the model again for another |
| `AgentSystem: this brain is still being prepared; …` | Await `prepareBrain` before `setBrain` |

### What ONNX Runtime costs

- **Download:** ONNX Runtime's WASM is 6.4 MB gzipped (25.7 MB), and its JavaScript 58 KB
  gzipped. This package's part, `OrtRuntime`, `OrtModel` and `OrtBrain`, is 3.1 KB min+gzip, paid
  only by apps that import them.
- **Start:** 0.8–0.9 s from the first line to the first actions in Chrome, and 1.3–1.6 s under
  Node: loading ONNX Runtime, making the device (0.5–0.7 s), and a model's first run, which
  compiles ONNX Runtime's pipelines (0.14–0.46 s). A second model starts in tens of milliseconds.
- **Each run,** for a 24→32→32→2 network over 20,000 agents: 0.5–1.3 ms of GPU time on an
  NVIDIA GPU and 1.5–1.7 ms on an AMD iGPU, 3× to 8× the built-in kernel's (up to 10× at 100,000
  agents). Run every frame, that is 8–10% of a 60 fps frame on the iGPU; `thinkEvery: 2` halves
  it. The main thread spends 0.6–0.8 ms per run.
- **`run()` can resolve well after the GPU is done.** ONNX Runtime checks for GPU errors in every
  run. In the test site's Herd & Wolves demo (Chrome, a worker, the trained 24→64→64→64→2
  networks), `run()` took 3–7 ms at 4,096–16,384 agents for 1–4 ms of GPU work, and 80–160 ms at
  65,536, where the GPU was busy. A timestamp written when `run()` resolves counts that wait.

## Current validation

- **Headless** (`npm run test:inference`): the reader gives back, bit for bit, what this
  repository's writer wrote, and one network written in 23 different ways. 13 files written by
  PyTorch 2.14.1 (both exporters), scikit-learn 1.7.2 and `onnx.helper` read with their makers'
  weights bit for bit; 3 are refused as they should be. 10,000 damaged files and every cut-short
  prefix of a file give a network or a named refusal, nothing else. `OrtRuntime`, `OrtModel` and
  `OrtBrain` run against a stand-in for ONNX Runtime: the options every session gets, each
  binding refusal, one run at a time, release after a run in flight, one call into ONNX Runtime at
  a time across models, in the order made, and that the real `onnxruntime-web` namespace
  type-checks as what `OrtRuntime.create` takes. This guide's two examples are type-checked and
  bundled; the reader's runs on the committed networks, and `useOrtBrain` on a stand-in engine.
- **On the GPU** (the `onnx` and `inference` suites), on Node/Dawn with an NVIDIA and an AMD GPU,
  and in Chrome, with ONNX Runtime Web 1.29.0:
  - for 17 files, the network read by `mlpFromOnnx` into an `MlpBrain` and ONNX Runtime running
    the same bytes give the same actions within 4.5e-6;
  - the runtime's device outlives every model, and a model released and loaded again runs;
  - PyTorch's two-file exports run with `externalData`, and agree with PyTorch within 4.8e-7;
  - Herd & Wolves with its prey on `OrtBrain` (A5): within 1.1e-5 of `MlpBrain` on the same step,
    with graph capture on and off; reruns byte-identical; switching brains with frames running;
  - 600 interactive frames (A6): no read-back outside the inspector, no WebGPU error, and the
    frame ages above;
  - `prepareBrain` (A33): `setBrain` of a prepared brain takes under 1 ms;
  - two models at once (A34): prey and wolves each on an `OrtBrain`, both loaded together and both
    runs started together, act as their networks say within 1.1e-5, with no WebGPU error.
- **ONNX Runtime 1.30.0** ran the `inference` suite under Node on an NVIDIA GPU only.
- **Not measured:** files from TensorFlow or Keras, and from reinforcement-learning libraries;
  export the policy as a plain PyTorch module. Models other than dense networks through
  `OrtBrain`: they run as ONNX Runtime runs them, but none is tested here.

Lights: Shader & Compute Reference
docs.text:
# Lights: Shader & Compute Reference This is the low-level companion to the [Lights API guide](./lights.md). It documents the exact memory layout of a light, the WGSL contract the `LightSystem` injects, and how to consume that layout **directly** — in a fully custom fragment shader or in your **own compute stage** — instead of going through `buildPBRShader`. Read [lights.md](./lights.md) first for the high-level flow. Everything here assumes you already have a `LightSystem` and its `lightStorageBuffer`. --- ## 1. Light memory layout (16 floats / 64 bytes) Every light is `LightSystem.FLOATS_PER_LIGHT` (16) floats — four `vec4`s. The proxies ([`PointLightProxy`](./lights.md) etc.) write into exactly these slots; if you build the buffer by hand (e.g. in a Worker) you must match this layout byte-for-byte. | vec4 | Float index | Field (WGSL) | Meaning | |---|---|---|---| | `pos_type` | 0, 1, 2 | `.xyz` | World position (point / spot / rectArea / torch)
Ground color (hemisphere) | | | 3 | `.w` | **Light type**: `1.0` point, `2.0` directional, `3.0` spot, `4.0` ambient, `5.0` hemisphere, `6.0` rectArea, `7.0` torch | | `col_int` | 4, 5, 6 | `.xyz` | Color RGB (linear) | | | 7 | `.w` | Intensity (multiplied into color) | | `dir_rad` | 8, 9, 10 | `.xyz` | Direction (directional / spot / hemisphere / rectArea / torch) | | | 11 | `.w` | Radius / range (point / spot / torch) | | `spot_params` | 12 | `.x` | `cos(innerConeAngle)` (spot / torch)
`width` (rectArea) | | | 13 | `.y` | `cos(outerConeAngle)` (spot / torch)
`height` (rectArea) | | | 14, 15 | `.zw` | Reserved
`flickerIntensity` (`.z`), `flickerSpeed` (`.w`) (torch) | ```wgsl struct Light { pos_type: vec4, col_int: vec4, dir_rad: vec4, spot_params: vec4, }; ``` > **Cone angles are stored as cosines.** `SpotLightProxy.innerConeAngle`/`outerConeAngle` call > `Math.cos()` on assignment. If you write the buffer manually, store `Math.cos(angle)`, not the > angle — the shader compares against `dot(...)` directly. ### Capacity and index assignment `capacity: { point, directional, spot, ambient, hemisphere, rectArea, torch }` only sizes the buffer — `totalLights` is their sum. There is **no enforced partitioning**: proxies `seek(index)` to any slot, and the shaders identify a light purely by its `pos_type.w` type flag. You own the index bookkeeping. A common scheme is to reserve a fixed range per type (e.g. directional at `[0, 4)`, points after), but any convention works as long as unused slots have a type your shader ignores. --- ## 2. The shader contract (`getShaderLayout`) `lights.getShaderLayout()` returns `{ wgslStructs, wgslLogic } | undefined`. The material shader builders splice these two strings in and then call the two functions the logic chunk defines. That is the entire contract — anything that provides these functions is a valid lighting backend: ```wgsl // Injected by wgslLogic — the two functions every material loop calls: fn getVisibleLightCount(worldPos: vec3) -> u32; fn getIncidentLight(index: u32, worldPos: vec3) -> IncidentLight; struct IncidentLight { color: vec3, // radiance (already color * intensity) direction: vec3, // unit vector from surface toward the light attenuation: f32, // distance + spot falloff, 1.0 for directional }; ``` The consuming loop in every lit material looks like this: ```wgsl let count = getVisibleLightCount(in.worldPos); for (var i = 0u; i < count; i = i + 1u) { let L = getIncidentLight(i, in.worldPos); // L.color, L.direction, L.attenuation → feed your BRDF } ``` - **`standard`** — `getVisibleLightCount` returns the total light count; `getIncidentLight` indexes `lights[index]` directly. - **`clustered-forward`** — `getVisibleLightCount` returns the per-cluster count for the pixel; `getIncidentLight` resolves `lightIndices[cluster.start_offset + i]` into `globalLights[...]`. Both paths return the identical `IncidentLight`, so a material shader is agnostic to which technique is active — swapping `standard` ↔ `clustered-forward` needs no shader change. ### Group 2 render bindings `applyToBatch(batch, groupIndex = 2)` binds these into the fragment shader's group: | Binding | `standard` | `clustered-forward` | |---|---|---| | 0 | `lights: array` | `globalLights: array` | | 1 | — | `clusterGrid: array` | | 2 | — | `lightIndices: array` | --- ## 3. Using the layout in a fully custom fragment shader You don't have to use `buildPBRShader`. Any WGSL shader can consume the lighting layout — just paste the struct/logic chunks in and honor the group-2 bindings. This is how you'd write a bespoke lit shader (custom BRDF, cheaper lighting, debug view, etc.): ```ts const layout = lights.getShaderLayout()!; // 'standard' or 'clustered-forward' const shaderCode = /* wgsl */ ` struct Camera { /* ...432-byte layout... */ }; @group(0) @binding(0) var camera: Camera; ${layout.wgslStructs} // Light / IncidentLight / Cluster + @group(2) bindings ${layout.wgslLogic} // getVisibleLightCount / getIncidentLight struct VertexOut { @builtin(position) clipPos: vec4f, @location(0) worldPos: vec3f, /* ... */ }; @fragment fn fs_main(in: VertexOut) -> @location(0) vec4f { let N = normalize(in.worldNormal); var lit = vec3f(0.0); let count = getVisibleLightCount(in.worldPos); for (var i = 0u; i < count; i = i + 1u) { let L = getIncidentLight(i, in.worldPos); lit += max(dot(N, L.direction), 0.0) * L.color * L.attenuation; // your own model } return vec4f(lit, 1.0); } `; const batch = engine.createBatch(scenePass, { shaderCode, strideFloats: 14, maxInstances: 1000, vertexLayouts: geom.layout.getWebGPUDescriptor(), }); lights.applyToBatch(batch, 2); // supplies the group-2 buffers the layout expects ``` > The **clustered** logic references `camera.view`, `camera.proj`, `camera.zNear`, `camera.zFar` — > so your shader must declare the full `Camera` struct (432-byte layout — see `src/core/Camera.ts` > or [Deprecated API §3](../deprecated-api.md)) and bind it at `@group(0) @binding(0)`. --- ## 4. Rolling your own compute stage over the light buffers `getComputeStage(camera)` builds the stock clustered binning stage. If you need custom binning, different culling math, or an extra pre-pass (e.g. clearing the cluster grid, which the stock stage notes it does not do), build your own `ComputeStageNode` against the same buffers. ### Buffers the `LightSystem` exposes | Property | WGSL type | Notes | |---|---|---| | `lightStorageBuffer` | `array` (read) | The 16-float-per-light data. | | `clusterGridBuffer` | `array` (read_write) | 2×`u32` per cluster: `start_offset`, `light_count`. | | `lightIndexBuffer` | `array` (read_write) | Flat list of light IDs, `totalClusters * maxLightsPerTile` long. | | `globalCounterBuffer` | `atomic` (read_write) | Bump allocator into `lightIndexBuffer`. | `clusterGridBuffer`, `lightIndexBuffer`, and `globalCounterBuffer` are only allocated when the technique is `clustered-forward`. `engine.ctx.cameraUniformBuffer` gives you the camera uniform. ### Binding layout the stock stage uses (group 0) ```wgsl @group(0) @binding(0) var camera: Camera; // engine.ctx.cameraUniformBuffer @group(0) @binding(1) var globalLights: array; // lightStorageBuffer @group(0) @binding(2) var clusterGrid: array; // clusterGridBuffer @group(0) @binding(3) var lightIndices: array; // lightIndexBuffer @group(0) @binding(4) var globalCounter: atomic; // globalCounterBuffer ``` ### Building the stage ```ts const grid = lights.config.clusterConfig!.grid; const totalClusters = grid[0] * grid[1] * grid[2]; const myBinning = engine.createComputeStage({ name: 'Custom Light Binning', shaderCode: myCullWGSL, // @workgroup_size(64,1,1), entry fn cs_main dispatchCount: [Math.ceil(totalClusters / 64), 1, 1], // Runs immediately before the dispatch — MUST reset the bump allocator each frame preClearBuffers: [ { buffer: lights.globalCounterBuffer!, offset: 0, data: new Uint32Array([0]) }, ], }); engine.setComputePassBindGroup(myBinning, [ { binding: 0, resource: { buffer: engine.ctx.cameraUniformBuffer } }, { binding: 1, resource: { buffer: lights.lightStorageBuffer } }, { binding: 2, resource: { buffer: lights.clusterGridBuffer! } }, { binding: 3, resource: { buffer: lights.lightIndexBuffer! } }, { binding: 4, resource: { buffer: lights.globalCounterBuffer! } }, ], 0); // Compute first, then the shading pass that reads the grid engine.render([myBinning, scenePass]); ``` ### What the stock binning kernel does (reference) The default `cs_main` (one invocation per cluster, 64 per workgroup): 1. Reconstruct the cluster's `(x, y, z)` from `global_id.x`; skip out-of-range invocations. 2. Compute an approximate bounding sphere for the cluster in **view space** using logarithmic depth slices (`zNear * (zFar/zNear)^(z/GRID_Z)`) and the camera FOV/aspect. 3. Loop over all `TOTAL_LIGHTS`: - **Directional** (`type == 2.0`) → always added (they affect every cluster). - **Point / spot** → transform position to view space and do a sphere-vs-sphere test against `clusterRadius + lightRadius`. 4. `atomicAdd(&globalCounter, visibleCount)` to reserve a contiguous slice, write `Cluster(offset, visibleCount)` into `clusterGrid[clusterIndex]`, then append the light IDs into `lightIndices[offset + i]`. The fragment side (§2, clustered) then reads `clusterGrid` for the pixel's cluster and walks `lightIndices` to fetch each `Light`. Your custom kernel only has to keep the same output contract — fill `clusterGrid` and `lightIndices` — and the stock fragment logic will consume it unchanged. > **Depth slicing is logarithmic.** Both the compute binning and the fragment `getClusterData` use > `log(depth / zNear) / log(zFar / zNear) * GRID_Z`. If you change the slicing in compute, mirror it > in your fragment lookup or lights will bin into the wrong cluster. --- ## 5. Gotchas - **Reset the counter every frame.** Without the `preClearBuffers` reset of `globalCounterBuffer`, `atomicAdd` keeps climbing and overflows `lightIndexBuffer` within a few frames. - **`maxLightsPerTile` is a hard cap.** The kernel stops adding lights to a cluster once it hits the cap, and it also bounds the total index buffer size. Size it for your worst-case local density. - **Only `clustered-forward` allocates the spatial buffers.** `standard` has `lightStorageBuffer` only; `getComputeStage` throws unless `clusterConfig` is present. - **Directional lights ignore culling** by design — they are unconditionally added to every cluster, so a scene with many directionals will inflate every cluster's count.

docs.title: Loaders API Usage
docs.text:
# Loaders API Usage

## First-Class GLTF / GLB Parsing
NullGraph includes a native `GLBParser` to ingest binary GLB assets. It unpacks vertex layouts,
indices, texture URLs, animation channels and skeletal data into engine-ready formats. It does
not currently preserve material colour factors or vertex colours.

```ts
import { GLBParser } from 'null-graph/loaders';

// Parse a GLB file directly into memory
const glbData = await GLBParser.load('./3dAssets/character.glb');

if (!glbData.meshes) throw new Error("No meshes found!");

// Easily map parsed mesh data to engine buffers
const vertexBuffer = engine.bufferManager.createVertexBuffer(glbData.meshes[0].vertices);
const indexBuffer = engine.bufferManager.createIndexBuffer(glbData.meshes[0].indices);
```

## Baked rigid animation (many instances, one shared table)

`bakeRigidAnimation` is for models animated by moving mesh nodes, not by skinning: a body,
head and legs as rigid parts. Use `GLBParser.load` or `parse`, **not `loadMerged`**: each mesh's
`node` identifies its entry in the parsed result's `nodes` hierarchy. Non-skinned vertices are
already transformed into model space at rest; those existing parser outputs are unchanged.

This complete preparation example is type-checked and run by `npm run test:loaders`:

```ts
import { GLBParser, bakeRigidAnimation } from 'null-graph/loaders';
import { MegabufferBuilder, StandardLayout } from 'null-graph/geometry';

export async function prepareRigidModel(url: string) {
    const glb = await GLBParser.load(url);
    const animation = bakeRigidAnimation(glb, {
        fps: 30,
        clips: ['idle', 'walk', 'run', { name: 'eat', loop: false }],
    });
    const mega = new MegabufferBuilder(StandardLayout.strideFloats);
    const mesh = mega.addMesh('animal', animation.vertices, animation.indices);
    const geometry = mega.build();

    // A vertex shader's vertex_index includes baseVertex. Pad to the whole mega vertex pool.
    const partOfVertex = new Uint32Array(geometry.megaVertices.length / StandardLayout.strideFloats);
    partOfVertex.set(animation.partOfVertex, mesh.baseVertex);
    const bounds = [0, 0, 0, animation.bounds.radius] as const;
    return { animation, mega, mesh, geometry, partOfVertex, bounds };
}
```

The result contains:
- `vertices`: rest-pose position, normal, uv (eight floats per vertex, `StandardLayout`);
  `indices`: `Uint32Array`; `vertexCount` and `indexCount`.
- `partOfVertex`: one `u32` per vertex; `parts`: the part count; `partNodes`: each part's node.
- `transforms`: frame-major, then part-major, **three rows of four floats** per transform.
  Part `p` in global frame `f` starts at `(f * parts + p) * 12`. Pose a position `v` with
  `dot(row0, vec4(v, 1))`, `dot(row1, vec4(v, 1))`, `dot(row2, vec4(v, 1))`.
  These are rest-to-pose transforms, not absolute node transforms.
- `clips`: `{ name, firstFrame, frames, seconds, loop }`; `frames`: total frames in the table.
- `bounds`: `min`, `max` and an origin-centred `radius` covering every sampled pose and convex
  blends of the table's poses. This does **not** bound the unsampled continuous glTF animation.

Options default to `fps: 30`, all clips in file order, looping, and `weld: true`. A looping clip
has `max(1, round(seconds * fps))` samples at `f * seconds / frames`; blend its last frame into
its first. A non-looping clip has `round(seconds * fps) + 1` samples including both endpoints
(one sample at zero if that count is one); clamp at the last frame. `firstFrame` is added after
selecting a frame within a clip. Linear blending of baked transforms approximates rotation
between samples: the test animals' run gait deviates by up to 37 mm at 30 fps. Raise `fps` for
closer motion, with a proportionally larger table.

Welding merges exact position, uv and part matches and averages/normalizes their normals; it
never joins different moving parts. Use `weld: false` to keep split face normals. A welded
flat-shaded model needs a fragment shader that reconstructs face normals from world-position
derivatives; otherwise it appears smooth. Under non-uniform scale, correct normal deformation
needs an inverse transpose: `GLBParser`'s existing rest-normal transform does not provide that.

The bake evaluates `LINEAR`, `STEP` and `CUBICSPLINE` channels and animated parents. It rejects
skinned meshes, missing mesh nodes or clips, empty clip selections, invalid fps, animated nodes
with a matrix, singular rest transforms and unknown interpolation modes. Morph-target weights
are not baked. The meshes become one material draw; separate material colours are not retained.

Upload `partOfVertex` and `animation.transforms` once as storage buffers shared by all instances.
Selecting clips/phases and deforming vertices is the application's shader's job; the bake alone
does not animate a draw. Use the instance-tier `vertexHook` in `null-graph/visibility` to apply
the table before the model transform (see the visibility guide). Skinned models use the
separate system below.

## Baked skinned animation (crowds)

`bakeSkinnedAnimation` is the four-influence companion to `bakeRigidAnimation`, exported from
`null-graph/loaders`. It evaluates the skeleton once at load time, not once per agent per frame.
The rigid bake and its one-influence format remain available unchanged.

```ts
import { GLBParser, bakeSkinnedAnimation } from 'null-graph/loaders';

export async function prepareSkinnedModel(url: string) {
    const glb = await GLBParser.load(url);
    try {
        const animation = bakeSkinnedAnimation(glb, { fps: 30 });
        return {
            animation,
            bounds: [0, 0, 0, animation.bounds.radius] as const,
        };
    } finally {
        // This example keeps geometry/animation only, not the source material textures.
        GLBParser.disposeImages(glb);
    }
}
```

Options and clip timing are the same as the rigid bake. The result has `vertices` (eight floats,
`StandardLayout`), `indices`, `vertexCount`, `indexCount`, `frames`, `clips` and `bounds`, plus:

- `influencesOfVertex`: four `u32` indices per vertex; unused slots have index and weight zero.
- `weightsOfVertex`: four `f32` weights per vertex, normalized to sum to one.
- `influences`: the table width; `influenceNodes`: the skin's joint nodes in their original order,
  followed by the nodes of rigid mesh attachments. An attachment has one influence of weight one.
- `transforms`: frame-major, influence-major, three rows of four floats. Influence `j` of frame `f`
  starts at `(f * influences + j) * 12`. Pose the vertex by summing the four transformed positions
  times their weights. Blend table rows linearly between frames, then blend clips as needed.

Skinning uses joint world transforms times inverse-bind matrices; the skinned mesh node's own
transform is ignored. To put bind-space geometry at the model's scale/orientation, the bake chooses
one fixed invertible transform `M` (the rest skinning matrix of the joint with the greatest total
weight), stores positions transformed by `M`, and stores `W(joint) * IBM(joint) * inverse(M)` in the
table. This preserves the exact weighted pose even if the file's default pose is not its bind pose;
in that case the stored vertices alone are **not** the default posed surface. Normals are transformed
by `M`'s inverse transpose and normalized; animated non-uniform scale still requires appropriate
normal deformation in the application. Bounds cover sampled weighted positions and convex blends,
not unsampled continuous motion. Welding requires exact position, UV, influence and weight matches.

The parser reads normalized `UNSIGNED_BYTE`/`UNSIGNED_SHORT` weights as floats and treats omitted
inverse-bind matrices as identity. The bake rejects multiple skins, additional influence sets
(`JOINTS_1`/`WEIGHTS_1`), zero-total, negative or non-finite weights, invalid joint indices, missing
nodes, malformed inverse binds, singular rebasing transforms, and the same invalid clip/timing
inputs as the rigid bake. Morph targets and separate material colours are not baked.

Upload influences, weights and the transform table once. When using a megabuffer, pad both per-vertex
arrays to its full vertex count and offset by `mesh.baseVertex * 4`, since `vertex_index` includes
the base vertex. This bake alone does not animate a draw. Use the palette snippets below to sample
once per **visible model**, after culling. The existing Herd & Wolves demo migration is phase 5.3;
the user's skinned animals follow when available.

## Baked pose / visible-model palette WGSL

Four independent strings are exported from `null-graph/loaders`:

| Export | Provides | Caller declares |
|---|---|---|
| `BAKED_POSE_WGSL` | `BakedPose { r0, r1, r2 }`, `bakedMix`, `bakedPosition`, `bakedNormal` | nothing |
| `BAKED_SAMPLE_WGSL` | `bakedFramePose`, `bakedClipPose` | storage-read `bakedTransforms: array<vec4<f32>>` |
| `BAKED_PALETTE_WRITE_WGSL` | `bakedWritePalette` | storage-read-write `bakedPalette: array<vec4<f32>>` |
| `BAKED_PALETTE_READ_WGSL` | `bakedPalettePose` (rigid), `bakedSkinPose` (four influences) | storage-read `bakedPalette: array<vec4<f32>>` |

Include the common pose string once in each shader module. The other strings require it and
declare no resources, entry points or bind groups. Apps own allocation, binding, clip selection,
dispatch, scheduling and teardown; no palette class or CPU work per visible agent is imposed.

Signatures (all functions are WGSL):

```wgsl
// tableBase and paletteBase are offsets in vec4 ROWS, not bytes or matrices.
// influences is the source table width; stride is the reserved influences per palette slot.
fn bakedFramePose(tableBase: u32, influences: u32, frame: u32, influence: u32) -> BakedPose
fn bakedClipPose(tableBase: u32, influences: u32, clip: vec2<u32>, phase: f32, looping: bool, influence: u32) -> BakedPose
fn bakedWritePalette(paletteBase: u32, stride: u32, slot: u32, influence: u32, pose: BakedPose)
fn bakedPalettePose(paletteBase: u32, stride: u32, slot: u32, influence: u32) -> BakedPose
fn bakedSkinPose(paletteBase: u32, stride: u32, slot: u32, joints: vec4<u32>, weights: vec4<f32>) -> BakedPose
fn bakedMix(a: BakedPose, b: BakedPose, weight: f32) -> BakedPose
fn bakedPosition(pose: BakedPose, position: vec3<f32>) -> vec3<f32>
fn bakedNormal(pose: BakedPose, normal: vec3<f32>) -> vec3<f32>
```

`clip` is `(firstFrame, frames)` from a baked clip. Phase is finite and measured in cycles, **not
seconds**: divide elapsed seconds by `clip.seconds` (use zero for a zero-duration clip). Looping
wraps negative/positive phases and interpolates across the seam. Non-looping clamps to `[0, 1]`
and includes the last frame. A one-frame clip holds its single pose. `bakedMix` does not clamp its
weight; keep blend weights in `[0, 1]` if relying on the bake's bounds. `bakedNormal` applies the
linear 3x3 part, without normalization or inverse transpose: normalize after transformation;
animated non-uniform scale needs application-specific normal handling or derivative face normals.

**Visible-slot scheduling with `VisibilitySystem`:** bind `batch.storageBuffer` as the compacted
`array<Instance>` and `batch.indirectBuffer` as storage-read `array<u32>`; `args[1]` is the count.
Dispatch enough threads for the batch capacity times its influence count; guard against that GPU
count before reading a survivor. Choose clips/phases from `visible[slot].sourceIndex`, sample each
influence and write its slot with `bakedWritePalette`. Put this stage **after that batch's cull and
before its draw**, e.g. `engine.render([...vis.getComputeStages(), paletteStage, scenePass])`.
Use separate palette regions/stages for batches (including separate camera/shadow culls).

In a vertex hook set **`instanceIndex: true`** and define the fifth argument `slot: u32`. Read the
palette by `slot`, never by `inst.sourceIndex`. For rigid vertices call
`bakedPalettePose(paletteBase, stride, slot, partOf[vi])`; for skinned vertices call
`bakedSkinPose(paletteBase, stride, slot, joints[vi], weights[vi])`, with indices and weights bound
as `array<vec4<u32>>` / `array<vec4<f32>>`. Return
`Deformed(bakedPosition(pose, pos), bakedNormal(pose, normal))`. Existing four-argument hooks remain
unchanged unless opted in. No vertex attributes, record layout or cull changes are needed.

**Memory and bounds are caller obligations:** reserve `capacity * stride * 48` bytes, plus any
base offset, with `STORAGE` usage (and `COPY_DST` if initializing). Capacity must cover the maximum
survivors, not just the previous frame's count; culling compacts the work but does not automatically
resize allocation. Check both `device.limits.maxStorageBufferBindingSize` and `maxBufferSize`, and
split batches/regions if required. Ensure all offsets/index products fit `u32`, `stride` covers all
influences, clips have at least one frame, and source/palette bounds are valid. Slots change every
cull and must be recomputed every frame; never reuse another view's slot assignment. Zero-weight
influences skip palette reads; weights should be non-negative and normalized. The snippets do not
validate malformed shader inputs or perform GPU allocation/dispatch for you.

**Executable examples:** `test/loaders-gpu/run.js` is a complete cull/palette/hook integration with
nonzero base offsets, clip blending, four-influence and rigid reads, shrinking/empty survivor lists,
and an independent CPU-rendered reference. Run `npm run test:gpu -- --only loaders`, or
`npm run test:gpu:browser -- --only loaders`. Build the library first.

## Hardware-Accelerated Skeletal Animations (one CPU-evaluated character)
NullGraph splits the heavy lifting: the CPU evaluates the animation timeline, and the GPU handles the vertex skinning. The `SkeletonManager` bridges the gap, allowing you to animate complex characters efficiently.

```ts
import { Animator, SkeletonManager } from 'null-graph/loaders';

// 1. Initialize animation systems with parsed GLB data
const skeletonManager = new SkeletonManager(engine.device, 70); // Max bones
const animator = new Animator(glbData.skin);
animator.play(glbData.animations[0]);

// 2. Bind the skeleton buffer to your mesh batch (Group 2)
engine.setRenderPassBindGroup(
    meshBatch,
    [{ binding: 0, resource: { buffer: skeletonManager.boneBuffer } }],
    2
);

// 3. Update loop
export function update(deltaTime: number) {
    // CPU computes the bone transforms ONCE
    animator.update(deltaTime);
    
    // GPU gets the updated bone matrices ONCE
    skeletonManager.updateFromAnimator(engine.device, animator);
}
```

docs.text:
# Materials API Usage

NullGraph ships a family of materials, from cheap unlit shading up to Cook-Torrance PBR. Each one
comes in two halves that you combine:

1. A **shader builder** (`build*Shader`) that assembles WGSL for the batch's pipeline. Builders take
   a `ShaderConfig` so you can toggle skinning (`useSkinning`), inject a lighting layout
   (`lighting`), and set material-specific options.
2. A **material class** that owns a uniform buffer + textures and binds them to the batch via
   `applyToBatch(batch)`.

```ts
import {
    buildPBRShader,     StandardPBRMaterial,
    buildBasicShader,   BasicMaterial,
    buildLambertShader, LambertMaterial,
    buildToonShader,    ToonMaterial,
    buildEmissiveShader, EmissiveMaterial,
    buildMatcapShader,  MatcapMaterial,
} from 'null-graph/materials';
```

> **Note:** the shader builders are plain functions — call `buildPBRShader({ ... })`, not
> `PBRShaderBuilder.build(...)`. (The source file was renamed from `ShaderBuilder.ts` to
> `PBRShaderBuilder.ts`, but the exported function name is unchanged. See
> [Deprecated API §7](../deprecated-api.md).)

---

## How materials work

Every material follows the same shape, so once you learn one you know them all:

```ts
// 1. Build the WGSL for the batch (skinning + optional lighting)
const shader = buildXShader({ useSkinning: false, lighting: lights?.getShaderLayout() });

// 2. Create the batch with that shader
const batch = engine.createBatch(pass, {
    shaderCode: shader,
    strideFloats: 14,
    maxInstances: 1000,
    vertexLayouts: geom.layout.getWebGPUDescriptor(),
});

// 3. Create the material and bind it (group index 1 by default)
const mat = new XMaterial(engine, { /* options */ });
mat.applyToBatch(batch);

// 4. Update params at runtime whenever you like
mat.updateUniforms({ /* changed fields */ });

// 5. Free the uniform buffer when done
mat.destroy();
```

**Texture fallbacks.** Every texture option is optional (except `MatcapMaterial.matcapMap`). When
omitted, the material substitutes a safe fallback from `engine.textureManager`
(`fallbackWhite` for color/packed maps, `fallbackNormal` for normal maps), and sets an internal
`hasX` flag so the shader ignores the fetch. A material never binds `null`.

**Updating parameters (the DOD way).** Materials keep their scalar params in a single small,
pre-allocated GPU uniform buffer. Mutating a public field (e.g. `mat.baseColor = [...]`) does **not**
touch the GPU on its own — call `updateUniforms(...)`, which re-packs the buffer and issues one
`writeBuffer`. There is no per-object allocation and no bind-group rebuild, so it's cheap to call
every frame. `applyToBatch` does **not** need to be called again after `updateUniforms`.

---

## Physically Based Rendering (Cook-Torrance PBR)

`StandardPBRMaterial` implements the Cook-Torrance BRDF with Albedo, Normal, and a **packed** map
carrying Ambient Occlusion / Roughness / Metallic.

```ts
const shaderCode = buildPBRShader({
    useSkinning: true,
    lighting: lightSystem.getShaderLayout(), // optional — omit for the built-in fallback light
});

const meshBatch = engine.createBatch(mainPass, {
    shaderCode,
    strideFloats: 14,
    maxInstances: 1000,
    vertexLayouts: geom.layout.getWebGPUDescriptor(),
});

const pbr = new StandardPBRMaterial(engine, {
    albedoMap: albedoView,
    normalMap: normalView,
    packedMap: armView,
    packedMapFormat: "ARM",        // 'ARM' (default) | 'MRAO'
    baseColor: [1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0],
    metallicMultiplier: 1.0,
    roughnessMultiplier: 1.0,
});

pbr.applyToBatch(meshBatch);
```

### Packed map format: `ARM` vs `MRAO`

The single "packed" texture stores three grayscale channels. Because different DCC tools and asset
stores pack them in different channel orders, `packedMapFormat` tells the shader how to read the RGB
channels — no need to re-author the texture.

| Format | R channel | G channel | B channel |
|---|---|---|---|
| `'ARM'` (default) | **A**mbient Occlusion | **R**oughness | **M**etallic |
| `'MRAO'` | **M**etallic | **R**oughness | **A**mbient Occlusion |

Roughness sits in G for both, so ARM and MRAO differ only in whether AO and Metallic are swapped
(R↔B). Pick the one matching your texture; the fragment shader branches on the flag at runtime:

```wgsl
// packedData = textureSample(texMRAO, samp, uv);
if (material.mapFormat < 0.5) {          // ARM
    ao = packedData.r; roughness *= packedData.g; metallic *= packedData.b;
} else {                                  // MRAO
    metallic *= packedData.r; roughness *= packedData.g; ao = packedData.b;
}
```

`metallicMultiplier` and `roughnessMultiplier` scale the sampled values (so a fully white packed map
plus multiplier `1.0` gives raw metallic/roughness of `1.0`).

### PBR options

| Option | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `albedoMap` | `GPUTextureView` | `fallbackWhite` | Base color texture. |
| `normalMap` | `GPUTextureView` | `fallbackNormal` | Tangent-space normal map. |
| `packedMap` | `GPUTextureView` | `fallbackWhite` | Packed AO/Roughness/Metallic map. |
| `packedMapFormat` | `'ARM' \| 'MRAO'` | `'ARM'` | Channel layout of `packedMap`. |
| `baseColor` | `[r,g,b,a]` | `[1,1,1,1]` | Multiplied onto albedo; alpha is output alpha. |
| `metallicMultiplier` | `number` | `1.0` | Scales sampled metallic. |
| `roughnessMultiplier` | `number` | `1.0` | Scales sampled roughness. |

**With no `packedMap`, the defaults make a rough metal.** The fallback map is white, so metallic and roughness are the
two multipliers themselves: both `1.0` by default. That is a fully metallic, fully rough surface with no diffuse term
(`kD *= 1.0 - metallic`), so it reads dark and grey under ordinary lights. For a painted or plastic surface, pass
`metallicMultiplier: 0` and a roughness such as `0.5`.

### Updating PBR params

PBR uses a **positional** update signature (the others use an options object):

```ts
pbr.updateUniforms(
    [1.0, 0.4, 0.1, 1.0], // baseColor
    0.9,                   // metallic
    0.3,                   // roughness
);
```

> Caveats: `updateUniforms` on PBR updates only `baseColor`, `metallic`, and `roughness`. It does
> **not** change the bound texture views, and it re-writes the packed-map format flag as `ARM`. If
> you rely on `MRAO`, prefer setting metallic/roughness through the multipliers at construction, or
> recreate the material to change textures/format.

### PBR bind-group layout (group 1)

| Binding | Resource |
|---|---|
| 0 | sampler |
| 1 | albedo texture |
| 2 | normal texture |
| 3 | packed (ARM/MRAO) texture |
| 4 | material uniform buffer (`baseColor`, `metallic`, `roughness`, `mapFormat`) |

---

## `BasicMaterial` — unlit

The cheapest material: no lights, no normal reads. Flat color or a single albedo texture, with
optional UV tiling for large surfaces.

```ts
const mat = new BasicMaterial(engine, {
    baseColor: [0.1, 0.5, 0.9, 1.0],
    albedoMap: albedoView,   // optional
    uvTiling: [4, 4],        // optional — tile the albedo across the surface
});

mat.updateUniforms({ baseColor: [1, 0, 0, 1], uvTiling: [8, 8] });
```

| Option / field | Type | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `baseColor` | `[r,g,b,a]` | `[1,1,1,1]` | Tint / flat color. |
| `albedoMap` | `GPUTextureView` | — (flat color) | Optional base texture. |
| `uvTiling` | `[u,v]` | `[1,1]` | Repeats the albedo map. |

`updateUniforms({ baseColor?, uvTiling? })` — omitted fields keep their current value.
**Bindings (group 1):** `0` sampler, `1` albedo, `2` uniform.

---

## `LambertMaterial` — cheap diffuse

Classic N·L diffuse with an ambient floor. The right pick for thousands of lit objects that don't
need specular. Pass a lighting layout into the builder; `useHalfLambert` softens the terminator.

```ts
const shader = buildLambertShader({ useSkinning: false, useHalfLambert: true, lighting });
const mat = new LambertMaterial(engine, {
    baseColor: [1, 1, 1, 1],
    albedoMap: albedoView,   // optional
    ambient: 0.15,           // prevents pitch-black shadows
});

mat.updateUniforms({ ambient: 0.25 });
```

| Option / field | Type | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `baseColor` | `[r,g,b,a]` | `[1,1,1,1]` | Diffuse albedo tint. |
| `albedoMap` | `GPUTextureView` | — (flat color) | Optional base texture. |
| `ambient` | `number` | `0.15` | Ambient light floor. |

`updateUniforms({ baseColor?, ambient? })` — omitted fields keep their current value.
**Bindings (group 1):** `0` sampler, `1` albedo, `2` uniform.

---

## `ToonMaterial` — cel shading

Banded (stepped) lighting with rim light and a specular threshold. The builder's `useSmoothRamp`
option swaps hard bands for a smooth ramp.

```ts
const shader = buildToonShader({ useSkinning: false, useSmoothRamp: false, lighting });
const mat = new ToonMaterial(engine, {
    baseColor: [0.9, 0.2, 0.3, 1.0],
    rampSteps: 4,
    rimLightColor: [1, 1, 1],
    rimLightPower: 2.0,
    specularThreshold: 0.7,
    albedoMap: albedoView,   // optional
    normalMap: normalView,   // optional
});

mat.updateUniforms({ baseColor: [0.9, 0.2, 0.3, 1.0], rampSteps: 3 });
```

| Option / field | Type | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `baseColor` | `[r,g,b,a]` | `[1,1,1,1]` | Surface color. |
| `rampSteps` | `number` | `3` | Number of shading bands. |
| `rimLightColor` | `[r,g,b]` | `[1,1,1]` | Fresnel rim tint. |
| `rimLightPower` | `number` | `2.0` | Rim falloff exponent. |
| `specularThreshold` | `number` | `0.5` | Cutoff for the toon specular blob. |
| `albedoMap` / `normalMap` | `GPUTextureView` | fallbacks | Optional textures. |

`updateUniforms({ baseColor?, rampSteps?, rimLightColor?, rimLightPower?, specularThreshold? })`.

> **Gotcha:** unlike the other materials, Toon's `updateUniforms` treats `baseColor` as
> **required** — if you omit it, the color resets to white `[1,1,1,1]`. Always pass `baseColor`
> when calling it.

**Bindings (group 1):** `0` sampler, `1` albedo, `2` normal, `3` uniform.

---

## `EmissiveMaterial` — glow / HDR

Self-illuminating surfaces, optionally pulsing over time. `emissiveIntensity` can exceed `1.0` to
feed a [Bloom](./post.md) pipeline. The pulse animates on the GPU from the camera's time slot — no
per-frame uniform write needed.

```ts
const mat = new EmissiveMaterial(engine, {
    baseColor: [0, 0, 0, 1],
    emissiveColor: [0.2, 0.9, 1.0],
    emissiveIntensity: 4.0,  // > 1.0 for HDR/Bloom
    emissiveMap: maskView,   // optional — masks which pixels glow
    pulseSpeed: 3.0,         // radians per simTime second
    pulseAmount: 0.5,        // 0 = steady, 1 = full pulse
});

mat.updateUniforms({ emissiveIntensity: 6.0 });
```

| Option / field | Type | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `baseColor` | `[r,g,b,a]` | `[0,0,0,1]` | Non-glowing base. |
| `emissiveColor` | `[r,g,b]` | `[1,1,1]` | Glow color, added on top. |
| `emissiveIntensity` | `number` | `1.0` | Glow strength; `>1.0` for HDR/Bloom. |
| `pulseSpeed` | `number` | `2.0` | Pulse rate (radians/sec). |
| `pulseAmount` | `number` | `0.0` | `0` steady … `1` full pulse. |
| `albedoMap` / `emissiveMap` | `GPUTextureView` | `fallbackWhite` | Optional textures. |

`updateUniforms({ baseColor?, emissiveColor?, emissiveIntensity?, pulseSpeed?, pulseAmount? })` —
omitted fields keep their current value.

> Pulsing reads `simTime` from the camera uniform — call
> `camera.updateTime(performance.now() * 0.001)` each frame before `engine.updateCamera(camera)`.

**Bindings (group 1):** `0` sampler, `1` albedo, `2` emissive, `3` uniform.

---

## `MatcapMaterial` — baked lighting

Material-capture shading: the whole lighting environment is baked into one sphere texture, looked up
by the view-space normal. Costs the same as an unlit material but reads as fully lit — great for
sculpt viewers, previews, and stylized crowds.

```ts
const mat = new MatcapMaterial(engine, {
    matcapMap: matcapView,   // required — the sphere-lit capture
    albedoMap: albedoView,   // optional — multiplied under the matcap
    baseColor: [1, 1, 1, 1],
});

mat.updateUniforms({ baseColor: [0.8, 0.9, 1.0, 1.0] });
```

| Option / field | Type | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `matcapMap` | `GPUTextureView` | **required** | The sphere-lit capture. |
| `albedoMap` | `GPUTextureView` | — | Optional, multiplied under the matcap. |
| `baseColor` | `[r,g,b,a]` | `[1,1,1,1]` | Tint. |

`updateUniforms({ baseColor? })`.
**Bindings (group 1):** `0` sampler, `1` matcap, `2` albedo, `3` uniform.

---

## Choosing a material

| Material | Lit? | Cost | Runtime-updatable params | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `BasicMaterial` | No | Lowest | `baseColor`, `uvTiling` | Flat colors, UI/debug, unlit props |
| `MatcapMaterial` | Baked | Very low | `baseColor` | Stylized/preview shading, no light setup |
| `LambertMaterial` | Yes (diffuse) | Low | `baseColor`, `ambient` | Massive counts of simple lit objects |
| `ToonMaterial` | Yes | Low–med | `baseColor`, `rampSteps`, rim, specular | Cel-shaded / NPR looks |
| `EmissiveMaterial` | Self | Low | color, intensity, pulse | Glowing cores, HDR sources for Bloom |
| `StandardPBRMaterial` | Yes (PBR) | Highest | `baseColor`, `metallic`, `roughness` | Photorealistic metal/dielectric surfaces |

To light any of the lit materials (`Lambert`, `Toon`, `PBR`), pass a `lighting` layout from the
[Lights](./lights.md) system into the builder and `applyToBatch` the `LightSystem` onto the same
batch. Omit `lighting` on the PBR builder to fall back to a single hardcoded key light.

## Things to know

Checked in 1.2.1's shader sources (`CommonChunks`, `materialFragments`, `PBRShaderCode`):

- **The instance's colour.** The stock vertex stage reads the 14-float instance: `[0]` pad, `[1..3]` position, `[4..7]`
  rotation quaternion (identity `w = 1`), `[8..10]` scale, `[11..13]` colour. Basic, Lambert, Toon, Emissive and Matcap
  multiply `baseColor` by that colour, so an instance whose colour is left at zero draws black. **PBR ignores the
  instance colour**: its colour is `baseColor` (times the albedo map) alone.
- **Scale, then rotate, then move.** Each vertex is scaled by the instance's scale in the shape's own axes, rotated by
  its quaternion, then offset by its position.
- **Only PBR tonemaps.** The PBR fragment ends with a Reinhard tonemap and a 1/2.2 gamma of its own. Basic, Lambert,
  Toon, Emissive and Matcap write linear colour. Under a post chain with `Tonemap`, PBR pixels are compressed twice. A
  target that mixes PBR with the others holds two encodings.
- **Lit or not.** Only Lambert, Toon and PBR read a `LightSystem`. Built with no `lighting` layout, each lights itself
  with one fixed key light from `(1, 1, 0.5)`. Basic, Emissive and Matcap ignore lights.
- **Faces.** Batches set no cull mode (`PipelineConfig` has none), so both faces of every triangle are drawn. A lit
  material shades a back face with its normal pointing away, so it draws dark.

docs.title: Night Sky API Usage
docs.text:
# Night Sky API Usage

Phase 3 of `null-graph/environment` adds three cooperating APIs:

- `NightSky` — the **resolved** night evaluator: lunar disc and phase, earthshine, night dome,
  airglow, Milky Way, and optional horizon light pollution;
- `SkyComposite` — decorates two `SkySource`s into the one `sampleSky` evaluator required by the
  environment bake and skybox;
- `StarField` — the **unresolved** point-source catalogue, rendered as one additive instanced draw.

The split is deliberate. The 0.52° moon is resolved by the source cube and therefore reaches SH
and specular IBL. A star is not resolved at any practical cube size, so it is drawn in screen space
with a fixed pixel footprint and does not enter the bake.

- **Environment and frame graph:** [`environment.md`](./environment.md)
- **Clock, moonlight, and sidereal rotation:** [`time-of-day.md`](./time-of-day.md)
- **Physical day atmosphere:** [`atmosphere.md`](./atmosphere.md)
- **Technical design:** [`environment-night-design.md`](../environment-night-design.md)
- **Sky shader contract:** [`environment-shader-reference.md`](./environment-shader-reference.md) §3.4

```ts
import {
    EnvironmentSystem,
    NightSky,
    PreethamSky,
    SkyComposite,
    StarField,
    TimeOfDay,
} from 'null-graph/environment';
```

---

## 1. Complete day/night setup

Install the resolved day/night evaluator before compiling the sky pass:

```ts
const env = new EnvironmentSystem(engine, {
    updateMode: 'amortized',
    keepSourceCube: true,
    prefilterMips: 6,
});

const night = new NightSky({
    nightGain: 1,
    latitudeDeg: 45,
    airglow: 0.00012,
    milkyWay: 0.0006,
    lightPollution: 0,
});

env.setSky(new SkyComposite({
    day: new PreethamSky({ turbidity: 2.8 }),
    night,
}));

const stars = new StarField(engine, {
    maxStars: 9100,
    latitudeDeg: 45,
    longitudeDeg: 0,
    radiusPx: 1.5,
    twinkle: 0.18,
});

const tod = new TimeOfDay({
    mode: 'artistic',
    latitudeDeg: 45,
    longitudeDeg: 0,
    timeScale: 60,
    rebakeThresholdDeg: 0.25,
    exposureCoupling: 'off',
    purkinje: true,
});
```

Create the environment sky pass, then attach the star batch. Batch insertion order is draw order,
so this puts the additive stars after the resolved sky evaluator:

```ts
const skyTarget = {
    colorAttachments,
```
