```ts
// Animals larger than 12 px on screen draw as the model, smaller ones as a cube: same rows.
vis.createInstanceDrawBatch(scenePass, 'cow', COW, { lod: { minPixels: 12 } });
vis.createInstanceDrawBatch(scenePass, 'cow-cube', COW, { lod: { maxPixels: 12 } });
```

Bounds are `minPixels` (inclusive) and `maxPixels` (exclusive); leave one out for an open end.
The far mesh needs its own `meshName` in the megabuffer but culls the near mesh's rows, so the
rows' bounds must cover both. Picking and shadows draw what their own batches say: a pick batch
over the same mesh index picks the full mesh at any size.

## 5. Render

```ts
function frame() {
    // (a worker may have written into instances.data)
    vis.setInstances(instances.data, instances.count);
    vis.upload();

    engine.render([
        lightBinning,                 // if using clustered lights
        ...vis.getComputeStages(),    // Hi-Z build + culls — MUST precede the scene pass
        scenePass,
        ...post.getPassSequence(),
    ]);
}
```

`getComputeStages()` returns a cached array and reads the shared camera uniform, so no per-call
camera is needed. Call `vis.resize(w, h)` alongside `engine.resize`, and `vis.destroy()` on
teardown.

## 6. Materials — the one-liner

Pass a stock material and you are done. Its WGSL (bindings + fragment) is generated and its
textures/uniform are bound automatically — **no shader code to write**:

```ts
import { StandardPBRMaterial } from 'null-graph/materials';

const rockMat = new StandardPBRMaterial(engine, { /* maps, baseColor, … */ });

const batch = vis.createInstanceDrawBatch(scenePass, 'rock', rock.meshIndex, {
    vertexLayouts: StandardLayout.getWebGPUDescriptor(),
    material: { kind: 'pbr', instance: rockMat },
});
```

With clustered lighting — the material's full lighting loop, still one line:

```ts
const batch = vis.createInstanceDrawBatch(scenePass, 'rock', rock.meshIndex, {
    vertexLayouts: StandardLayout.getWebGPUDescriptor(),
    material: { kind: 'pbr', instance: rockMat, lighting: lights.getShaderLayout() },
});
lights.applyToBatch(batch, 2);   // bind the light buffers at group 2
```

`kind` is one of `'basic' | 'lambert' | 'emissive' | 'matcap' | 'toon' | 'pbr'` and must match the
material instance's family. It is explicit rather than sniffed from the class so
`null-graph/visibility` never has to import `null-graph/materials` at runtime.

| Field | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `kind` | which stock family (selects the WGSL) |
| `instance` | the material object; its `applyToBatch` binds the resources |
| `lighting` | `lights.getShaderLayout()` — enables the material's clustered/tiled loop |
| `useHalfLambert` | Lambert only — wrap light around the terminator |
| `useSmoothRamp` | Toon only — soften the cel ramp |

**Groups are handled for you.** Instance tier binds the material at group 1; meshlet tier at
group 2 (group 1 holds the meshlet geometry there), and the generated WGSL uses the matching index.
Override with `materialGroupIndex` — e.g. `3` on the meshlet tier if you also want lighting at 2.

Works identically on the meshlet tier:

```ts
vis.createMeshletDrawBatch(scenePass, { material: { kind: 'lambert', instance: rockMat } });
```

**Custom shaders still win.** Supplying `fragmentBody` overrides `material` entirely, so a
hand-written shader is never second-guessed. See
[shader reference §4](./visibility-shader-reference.md#4-using-a-built-in-material-with-a-culled-batch)
for the manual route and the exact WGSL contract.

Why this works: the visibility `VertexOut` is **field-identical** to the material contract
(`worldPos`/`worldNormal`/`uv`/`ecsColor`), and both modules compose their fragment stage from the
same `materials/materialFragments.ts` — so a material can never disagree with itself. Guarded by
`npm run test:visibility`.

## 7. Hi-Z occlusion

Omit `hiZ` to run frustum + cone culling only. To add occlusion, supply a **samplable** depth
texture (`TEXTURE_BINDING`) that the pyramid is rebuilt from each frame.

- `ctx.depthTexture` is `RENDER_ATTACHMENT`-only and **cannot** be used. Supply a depth pre-pass
  target or the `PostChain` g-buffer depth.
- The pyramid is built from **last frame's** depth (single-phase), so a fast camera cut can briefly
  disocclude geometry for one frame. Frame 0 — and the first frame after a resize — occludes
  nothing: a depth footprint of exactly 0 (a never-rendered, zero-initialized texture) is treated as
  "no history". Pinned on a GPU by `test/visibility-gpu` V3a; before Cycle A it culled *everything*.
- Per-instance opt-out: `INSTANCE_FLAG_NO_OCCLUSION`.

## 8. Post-Processing Presets Integration

`VisibilitySystem` draw passes integrate directly with `PostChain` and stylized post-processing presets (such as `ChainPresets.anime()`).

```ts
import { VisibilitySystem } from 'null-graph/visibility';
import { PostChain, ChainPresets } from 'null-graph/post';

// 1. Setup PostChain with G-Buffer depth enabled for outline/silhouette rendering
const post = new PostChain(engine, {
  format: 'rgba16float',
  gbuffer: { depth: 'depth24plus' },
  outputToScreen: true,
});
post.setChain(ChainPresets.anime());

// 2. Main scene pass consumes post scene attachments
const scenePass = engine.createPass({
  name: 'Visibility Main Pass',
  isMainScreenPass: false,
  ...post.sceneAttachments({ clearValue: { r: 0.01, g: 0.012, b: 0.02, a: 1.0 } }),
});

// 3. Create draw batch matching the PostChain format
vis.createMeshletDrawBatch(scenePass, {
  targetFormat: post.format,
  fragmentBody: `...`,
});

// 4. Return compute stages, main pass, and post chain sequence in update()
return [
  ...vis.getComputeStages(),
  scenePass,
  ...post.getPassSequence(),
];
```

## 9. Errors (fail-loud, at build/compile time)

| Condition | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `mode: 'two-phase'` | throws (reserved for a later build) |
| `maxInstances < 1` | throws |
| `setInstances` count > `maxInstances` | throws |
| `setInstanceCount` count > `maxInstances`, negative or not a whole number | throws |
| instance-tier batch before `setGeometry(mega)` | throws |
| meshlet tier without `setGeometry(mega, pack)` | throws |
| meshlet tier without `maxMeshletsPerInstance` / `maxVisibleMeshletInstances` | throws |
| `getComputeStages()` before any draw batch | throws |
| `lod` with neither bound, a bound that is not a finite number ≥ 0, or `minPixels` ≥ `maxPixels` | throws, before the batch is made |

## 10. Notes & limits

- **Two-phase mode is reserved.** Single-phase is the proven baseline (design §13 build order).
- **No CPU readback.** Nothing stalls the pipeline to read a GPU counter; dispatch sizes come from
  CPU-known caps with idle threads early-outing.
- **Meshlet-tier group 2 collision.** The material defaults to group 2 there, which is also
  `lights.applyToBatch(batch, 2)`. Use `materialGroupIndex: 3` if you need both.
- **`maxVisibleMeshletInstances` is not bounds-checked on the GPU.** Under-sizing it overflows the
  compaction buffer. Budget generously.
- **Testing.** The pure cull math (frustum, sphere, cone, Hi-Z level, LOD) and every generated WGSL
  module are covered headless by `npm run test:visibility`. On a real device, `test/visibility-gpu`
  (run by `npm run test:gpu` / `test:gpu:browser`) pins one draw per mesh at any instance count, the
  GPU cull against the CPU mirror, Hi-Z occlusion, the vertex hook, and LOD bands (each row drawn
  by exactly one band, as the CPU mirror of its size says); the meshlet-tier scenes are not written
  yet.

# Visibility — Shader & Buffer Reference

Companion to [`visibility.md`](./visibility.md) (usage) and
[`visibility-design.md`](../visibility-design.md) (architecture). This is the **contract layer**:
exact byte layouts, WGSL bindings, the generated kernels, and how to plug a material into a
GPU-culled draw.

Read this when you are writing a custom draw shader, debugging a bind-group error, filling
instance data from a worker, or wiring a built-in material into a visibility batch.

---

## 1. Buffer layouts

Every structure is 16-byte aligned, `vec4`-shaped, and worker-fillable. Sizes are exact.

### 1.1 `Instance` — 96 bytes (24 floats)

The per-frame input you fill. Written via `InstanceBuffer.write()`, or by a Web Worker writing
the raw arrays directly.

| Float | Bytes | Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0–15 | 0–63 | `model` | `mat4x4<f32>` | **Column-major** object→world matrix (gl-matrix `mat4`). |
| 16–19 | 64–79 | `boundsCenter` | `vec4<f32>` | Object-space bounding sphere: `.xyz` center, `.w` radius. |
| 20 | 80 | `meshIndex` | `u32` | Index into `meshTable`. Instance tier also uses it to route instances to the matching draw batch. |
| 21 | 84 | `lodOverride` | `u32` | Relative LOD level (0 = finest), or `LOD_AUTO` (`0xFFFFFFFF`). |
| 22 | 88 | `flags` | `u32` | Bit 0 `INSTANCE_FLAG_NO_OCCLUSION`, bit 1 `INSTANCE_FLAG_NO_CONE_CULL`. |
| 23 | 92 | `_pad` | `u32` | Must be 0. |

The integer fields occupy float slots but hold **raw u32 bits** — write them through a
`Uint32Array` view over the same `ArrayBuffer`, which is exactly what `InstanceBuffer` does. Writing
`20.0` as a float into slot 20 does *not* mean `meshIndex == 20`.

```ts
// Worker-side, no engine import needed — just the layout.
const INSTANCE_FLOATS = 24;
const f32 = new Float32Array(sab);          // shared with the main thread
const u32 = new Uint32Array(sab);           // SAME memory, integer view
const base = i * INSTANCE_FLOATS;
f32.set(modelMatrix, base);                 // 16 floats, column-major
f32[base + 16] = cx; f32[base + 17] = cy; f32[base + 18] = cz; f32[base + 19] = radius;
u32[base + 20] = meshIndex;
u32[base + 21] = 0xFFFFFFFF;                // LOD_AUTO
u32[base + 22] = 0;                         // flags
u32[base + 23] = 0;
```

### 1.2 `Meshlet` — 64 bytes

Produced by `MeshletBuilder`; read-only at runtime.

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `boundsCenter` | `vec4<f32>` | Object-space sphere (`.xyz` center, `.w` radius) for frustum + Hi-Z. |
| `coneApex` | `vec4<f32>` | `.xyz` cone apex (the sphere center in v1). `.w` unused. |
| `coneAxis` | `vec4<f32>` | `.xyz` normalized axis, `.w` = **cutoff**. `cutoff >= 2.0` is the "never cull" sentinel. |
| `offsets` | `vec4<u32>` | `.x` vertexOffset, `.y` triangleOffset, `.z` vertexCount, `.w` triangleCount. |

### 1.3 `MeshEntry` / `MeshLOD` — 16 bytes each

| `MeshEntry` | Type | | `MeshLOD` | Type |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `lodOffset` | `u32` | | `meshletOffset` | `u32` |
| `lodCount` | `u32` | | `meshletCount` | `u32` |
| `_pad0`, `_pad1` | `u32` | | `error` | `f32` (world-space geometric error) |
| | | | `_pad` | `f32` |

### 1.4 `VisibleInstance` — 16 bytes (internal)

Meshlet-tier intermediate, written by pass 1 and read by pass 2:
`{ instanceId: u32, lodMeshletOffset: u32, lodMeshletCount: u32, _pad: u32 }`.

### 1.5 `CullParams` — 32 bytes (uniform, per cull stage)

Refreshed every frame by `upload()`.

| Field | Type | Source |
|---|---|---|
| `instanceCount` | `u32` | `setInstances(..., count)` or `setInstanceCount(n)` |
| `meshIndex` | `u32` | the batch's mesh (instance tier); 0 for meshlet tier |
| `hizMaxLevel` | `u32` | `HiZPyramid.maxLevel` |
| `flags` | `u32` | reserved (0) |
| `screenSize` | `vec2<f32>` | `hiZ.width/height`, else canvas size |
| `lodErrorPx` | `f32` | `config.lodErrorPx` (default 1.0) |
| `_pad` | `f32` | 0 |

### 1.6 Indirect draw args — 20 bytes (5 × u32)

Engine-allocated (`BatchManager.ts:61-64`). The layout `drawIndexedIndirect` consumes:

```
[0] indexCount      written once by VisibilitySystem at batch creation
[1] instanceCount   ZEROED each frame via preClearBuffers, then atomically bumped by the cull
[2] firstIndex      per-mesh (instance tier) / 0 (meshlet tier)
[3] baseVertex      per-mesh (instance tier) / 0 (meshlet tier)
[4] firstInstance   0
```

Slot `[1]` is the whole GPU-driven trick: the cull kernel's `atomicAdd(&drawArgs[1], 1u)` both
allocates a compaction slot **and** grows the draw. No CPU readback.

---

## 2. Bind-group contracts

`layout: 'auto'` prunes any binding the shader does not *use*, and supplying an entry for a pruned
binding throws. The generated kernels therefore declare a binding **only** when the corresponding
feature is enabled — which is why occlusion-off variants omit `params`/`hiz` entirely.

### 2.1 Cull kernels (group 0)

| Binding | Instance cull | Meshlet instance cull (pass 1) | Meshlet cull (pass 2) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | camera | camera | camera |
| 1 | instances (read) | instances (read) | instances (read) |
| 2 | outInstances (rw) | visibleInstances (rw) | visibleInstances (read) |
| 3 | drawArgs (atomic) | counters (atomic) | meshlets (read) |
| 4 | params | meshTable (read) | counters (atomic) |
| 5 | *hiz* † | meshLODs (read) | outMeshlets (rw) |
| 6 | — | params | drawArgs (atomic) |
| 7 | — | *hiz* † | *params* † |
| 8 | — | — | *hiz* † |

† emitted only when Hi-Z occlusion is enabled. Note pass 2 declares **`params` only under
occlusion** — nothing else in that kernel reads it.

### 2.2 Draw shaders

**Instance tier** — group 0 is fixed by `createBatch` (`BatchManager.ts:73-79`):

| Group | Binding | Resource |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0 | `camera` (uniform) |
| 0 | 1 | `instances` — the **compacted survivors** (`batch.storageBuffer`) |
| 1+ | — | your material (`materialEntries`, default group 1) |
| 2 | — | lighting, if you call `lights.applyToBatch(batch, 2)` |

**Meshlet tier** — group 1 is occupied by geometry, so materials move up:

| Group | Binding | Resource |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0 | `camera` |
| 0 | 1 | `visible: array<vec2<u32>>` — `{instanceId, meshletId}` (`batch.storageBuffer`) |
| 1 | 0–4 | `meshlets`, `meshletVertices`, `meshletTriangles`, `megaVertices`, `instances` |
| 2+ | — | your material (`materialGroupIndex`, default 2) |

> **Group 2 collision.** On the meshlet tier the material defaults to group 2, which is also where
> `LightSystem.applyToBatch(batch, 2)` binds. If you want both, pass an explicit
> `materialGroupIndex: 3` and bind lighting at 2. On the instance tier there is no collision:
> material at 1, lighting at 2, exactly as the stock material shaders expect.

---

## 3. The `VertexOut` contract

Both draw shaders emit a struct that is **field-identical to `materials/CommonChunks.ts`**:

```wgsl
struct VertexOut {
    @builtin(position) clipPos: vec4<f32>,
    @location(0) worldPos: vec3<f32>,
    @location(1) worldNormal: vec3<f32>,
    @location(2) uv: vec2<f32>,
    @location(3) ecsColor: vec3<f32>,
};
```

This match is deliberate and load-bearing: it is what lets a stock material's fragment shader drop
into a visibility batch **unchanged** (§4). `ecsColor` is filled with white because the visibility
`Instance` record carries no per-instance color, so `material.baseColor * instanceColor` reduces to
`material.baseColor` — the correct no-tint result.

The normal is transformed by the inverse-transpose of the model's upper 3×3
(`normalMatrixFromModel`) and renormalized, so non-uniformly scaled instances shade correctly.

---

## 4. Using a built-in material with a culled batch

The default fragment is a neutral hemispheric shade — fine for bring-up, not for real rendering.

### 4.0 The one-liner (preferred)

Pass a stock material; the WGSL and the bind group are generated for you:

```ts
vis.createInstanceDrawBatch(scenePass, 'rock', rock.meshIndex, {
    vertexLayouts: StandardLayout.getWebGPUDescriptor(),
    material: { kind: 'pbr', instance: rockMat, lighting: lights.getShaderLayout() },
});
```

Under the hood this calls `buildMaterialFragment({ kind, groupIndex, lighting })` from
`materials/materialFragments.ts` — **the single source of truth** that the stock full-shader
builders (`buildPBRShader`, `buildLambertShader`, …) also compose from. One definition of each
material's bindings and `fs_main`, two consumers, so they cannot drift.

```ts
import { buildMaterialFragment } from 'null-graph/materials';

const { bindings, fragment } = buildMaterialFragment({ kind: 'lambert', groupIndex: 1 });
// bindings → struct + @group(1) declarations (+ helper math, + lighting when supplied)
// fragment → the material's @fragment fn fs_main
```

The rest of this section documents the **manual** route — what the one-liner generates. Use it
when you want a custom fragment, a non-stock material, or to understand the contract.

### 4.1 Instance tier — groups already line up

The stock material bindings sit at `@group(1)` and lighting at `@group(2)` — precisely the instance
tier's defaults. So the material's own WGSL needs no group edits:

```ts
import { StandardLayout } from 'null-graph/geometry';

const MATERIAL_BINDINGS = /* wgsl */ `
    struct LambertMaterialParams {
        baseColor: vec4<f32>,
        ambient: f32,
        hasAlbedoTexture: f32,
        _pad: vec2<f32>,
    };
    @group(1) @binding(0) var samp: sampler;
    @group(1) @binding(1) var texAlbedo: texture_2d<f32>;
    @group(1) @binding(2) var<uniform> material: LambertMaterialParams;
`;

const MATERIAL_FRAGMENT = /* wgsl */ `
@fragment
fn fs_main(in: VertexOut) -> @location(0) vec4<f32> {
    var baseColor = material.baseColor * vec4<f32>(in.ecsColor, 1.0);
    if (material.hasAlbedoTexture > 0.5) {
        baseColor = textureSample(texAlbedo, samp, in.uv) * baseColor;
    }
    let N = normalize(in.worldNormal);
    let L = normalize(vec3<f32>(1.0, 1.0, 0.5));
    let NdotL = max(dot(N, L), 0.0);
    let finalColor = material.ambient * baseColor.rgb + baseColor.rgb * NdotL;
    return vec4<f32>(finalColor, baseColor.a);
}`;

const batch = vis.createInstanceDrawBatch(scenePass, 'rock', rock.meshIndex, {
    vertexLayouts: StandardLayout.getWebGPUDescriptor(),
    extraBindings: MATERIAL_BINDINGS,      // declared in the generated module
    fragmentBody: MATERIAL_FRAGMENT,       // replaces the default fragment
    materialEntries: [                     // bound at group 1
        { binding: 0, resource: sampler },
        { binding: 1, resource: albedoView },
        { binding: 2, resource: { buffer: materialParamsBuffer } },
    ],
});
```

`extraBindings` and `fragmentBody` are two halves of one thing — the WGSL *declarations* and the
WGSL *body*. Supplying a fragment that references bindings you did not declare is a shader-creation
error, which fails loudly at batch creation.

### 4.2 Adding clustered lighting

The stock material fragments call `getVisibleLightCount()` / `getIncidentLight()`, which
`LightSystem.getShaderLayout()` emits. Concatenate them into `extraBindings`, and bind the light
buffers at group 2:

```ts
const layout = lights.getShaderLayout()!;   // clustered-forward or standard
const batch = vis.createInstanceDrawBatch(scenePass, 'rock', rock.meshIndex, {
    vertexLayouts: StandardLayout.getWebGPUDescriptor(),
    extraBindings: MATERIAL_BINDINGS + layout.wgslStructs + layout.wgslLogic,
    fragmentBody: LIT_FRAGMENT,             // the loop form, as in buildLambertShader
});
lights.applyToBatch(batch, 2);
```

### 4.3 Meshlet tier — shift the material group

Identical, except the material cannot use group 1 (geometry lives there). Pass
`materialGroupIndex: 2` (or 3 alongside lighting) and change `@group(1)` to the matching index in
`MATERIAL_BINDINGS`. This is the one place the stock material WGSL needs an edit.

### 4.4 How the two paths share one definition

```
                materials/materialFragments.ts
                  MaterialBindings[kind](group)
                  MaterialFragments[kind](config)
                  buildMaterialFragment(...)
                          │
            ┌─────────────┴──────────────┐
            ▼                            ▼
  buildPBRShader / buildLambertShader   VisibilitySystem
  (+ engine bindings, ECS vertex        (+ GPU-culled vertex stage reading
   stage reading the 14-float buffer)    a mat4 from the Instance record)
```

Both paths emit the **same** `VertexOut` (§3) and the **same** fragment stage; only the vertex
stage and the group index differ. `npm run test:visibility` asserts the `VertexOut` parity and that
every family composes into both tiers without a binding collision — so this cannot silently rot.

The remaining nuance is the meshlet tier's group 2 default (§4.3): pass `materialGroupIndex: 3` if
you want a material *and* clustered lighting on that tier.

---

## 5. Generated kernels

Every generator is exported, so you can print one and read it — the fastest way to debug a
bind-group mismatch.

| Function | Emits |
|---|---|
| `buildHiZMipWGSL(fromDepth)` | one Hi-Z mip reduction (max of 2×2) |
| `buildInstanceCullWGSL({occlusion})` | instance tier cull + compaction |
| `buildMeshletInstanceCullWGSL({occlusion})` | meshlet pass 1: coarse cull + LOD select |
| `buildMeshletCullWGSL({occlusion, cone})` | meshlet pass 2: per-cluster cull + compaction |
| `buildInstanceDrawWGSL(opts)` | instance tier draw (standard indexed-instanced) |
| `buildMeshletDrawWGSL(opts)` | meshlet tier draw (vertex pulling) |

Reusable chunks: `CAMERA_STRUCT_WGSL`, `INSTANCE_STRUCT_WGSL`, `MESHLET_STRUCT_WGSL`,
`MESH_TABLE_STRUCT_WGSL`, `CULL_PARAMS_WGSL`, `CULL_CORE_WGSL`, `HIZ_OCCLUSION_WGSL`.

```ts
import { buildInstanceCullWGSL } from 'null-graph/visibility';
console.log(buildInstanceCullWGSL({ occlusion: true }));
```

### 5.1 Dispatch shapes

| Stage | Workgroup | Dispatch |
|---|---|---|
| Hi-Z mip | `(8, 8, 1)` | `ceil(mipW/8) × ceil(mipH/8)` |
| Instance cull | `(64, 1, 1)` | `ceil(instanceCount/64)` — re-evaluated per frame |
| Meshlet pass 1 | `(64, 1, 1)` | `ceil(instanceCount/64)` |
| Meshlet pass 2 | `(8, 8, 1)` | `ceil(maxInstances/8) × ceil(maxMeshletsPerInstance/8)` |

Pass 2 dispatches over **CPU-known caps**, not the GPU-side visible count, and idle lanes early-out
against `counters[0]` / `lodMeshletCount`. That is the deliberate cost of never stalling on a
readback; indirect dispatch would remove it (design §12).

---

## 6. The cull math, and the signs that matter

Mirrored exactly between `cullMath.ts` (CPU, unit-tested) and `CULL_CORE_WGSL` (GPU). The CPU copy
exists so these can be pinned by numbers headlessly — run `npm run test:visibility`.

### 6.1 Frustum — the ZO near plane

NullGraph's camera uses `mat4.perspectiveZO`, so NDC z spans **[0, 1]**, not [-1, 1]:

```
L = r3 + r0    R = r3 - r0    B = r3 + r1    T = r3 - r1
N = r2         ← ZO form (clip z >= 0). NOT r3 + r2, which is the OpenGL [-1,1] form.
F = r3 - r2
```

Using the OpenGL near plane halves the near distance and culls geometry that is actually visible.

### 6.2 Normal cone

```wgsl
if (cutoff >= 2.0) { return false; }          // sentinel: too wide to ever cull
let d = normalize(apexW - eye);               // camera → apex, NOT the negation
return dot(normalize(axisW), d) >= cutoff;    // >=, not <=
```

Flip either the comparison or the direction and you cull exactly the **visible** clusters — holes
where geometry should be. Covered by test U4.

### 6.3 Hi-Z occlusion

```wgsl
return ndcNear > occ;   // sphere's nearest point is behind the farthest occluder
```

The pyramid stores the **max** (farthest) depth per 2×2 block, because the depth buffer holds the
*nearest* surface per pixel and an object is hidden only when it is behind the farthest of those.
No depth remap is needed: the pyramid and `ndcNear` come from the same ZO projection. A near-plane
guard keeps anything straddling the near plane visible.

---

## 7. Frame cost

The complete per-frame CPU work, with no allocation:

```ts
vis.setInstances(instances.data, instances.count);  // adopt by reference — no copy
vis.upload();                                       // 1 writeBuffer + params refresh per stage
engine.render([...vis.getComputeStages(), scenePass, ...post.getPassSequence()]);
```

`getComputeStages()` returns a **cached** array (rebuilt only when geometry or batches change).
`preClearBuffers` zeroes `drawArgs[1]` and `counters[0]` before each stage. Everything else —
plane extraction, culling, compaction, LOD — happens on the GPU.

---

## 8. Debugging checklist

| Symptom | Likely cause |
|---|---|
| Nothing renders | `getComputeStages()` not spliced **before** the scene pass; or `upload()` not called, so `instanceCount` is 0. |
| Everything renders (no culling) | Instances' `boundsCenter` radius is 0 or wrong — a zero-radius sphere fails the frustum test only when fully outside. Verify with `worldSphereFromModel`. |
| Holes / geometry vanishes when the camera turns | Cone sign inverted, or `coneAxis.w` not the `sin(α)` cutoff (geometry doc §6.2). |
| Everything vanishes once Hi-Z is on | `ndcNear > occ` flipped, or the depth source is not the *previous* frame's. |
| Bind-group creation throws | A declared-but-unused binding was pruned by `layout: 'auto'` — check the §2.1 table for the occlusion-off variant. |
| Meshlets flicker at distance | `maxVisibleMeshletInstances` too small; the compaction overflowed. Raise it. |
| Shading is black / inside-out | Custom `fragmentBody` reading `in.normal` — the field is **`worldNormal`** (§3). |

# NullGraph A data-oriented WebGPU rendering library with explicit render and compute scheduling, flat instance data, and optional GPU-driven rendering and simulation modules.
[![npm version](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/null-graph?style=for-the-badge&color=33e6cc&labelColor=0a0a0a)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/null-graph) [![npm downloads](https://img.shields.io/npm/dm/null-graph?style=for-the-badge&color=ff6b6b&labelColor=0a0a0a)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/null-graph) [![bundle size](https://img.shields.io/bundlephobia/minzip/null-graph?style=for-the-badge&color=fcc419&labelColor=0a0a0a)](https://bundlephobia.com/package/null-graph) [![license: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-51cf66?style=for-the-badge&labelColor=0a0a0a)](./LICENSE) [![stars](https://img.shields.io/github/stars/Vikas593-cloud/NullGraph?style=for-the-badge&color=ff922b&labelColor=0a0a0a)](https://github.com/Vikas593-cloud/NullGraph/stargazers)
NullGraph has no retained scene graph. Applications supply geometry, buffers, batches and an ordered sequence of compute stages and render passes. This makes resource ownership and execution order explicit, and lets GPU simulation output feed rendering without a per-frame CPU readback. It can run on the main thread, in a Web Worker with an `OffscreenCanvas`, or headlessly with a WebGPU implementation. The repository also includes offline rendering tools: fixed-step scene recording, GPU-state tracks, checkpoints, replay, and frame export to PNG or ffmpeg video, independent of real-time frame rate. The agent APIs provide GPU policy tables, species-specific brains, and explicit stepping for application-defined population evaluation, co-evolution, and historical-opponent comparisons. ## Installation and getting started ```sh npm install null-graph ``` Import the core and the modules your application needs: ```ts import { NullGraph, Camera } from 'null-graph'; import { Primitives, StandardLayout } from 'null-graph/geometry'; import { StandardPBRMaterial } from 'null-graph/materials'; ``` - [Application guide and runnable examples](https://github.com/Vikas593-cloud/NullGraph/blob/master/docs/agent/guide.md) - [Core setup and usage](https://github.com/Vikas593-cloud/NullGraph/blob/master/docs/api/core.md) - [Core API and buffer reference](https://github.com/Vikas593-cloud/NullGraph/blob/master/docs/api/core-reference.md) - [Documentation index for coding assistants](https://github.com/Vikas593-cloud/NullGraph/blob/master/llms.txt) The application guide includes complete examples and a render-to-PNG workflow. Its tooling runs from a repository checkout; the npm package ships the library's `dist/` files, not the repository runners. Branch-head documentation may describe changes newer than your installed package; match documentation to the release or commit you use. ## Rendering model - **Flat data rather than scene traversal.** Instance transforms and attributes live in typed arrays or GPU buffers. Applications manage hierarchy and gameplay state themselves. - **Explicit scheduling.** Submit a linear sequence of compute stages and render passes, including multipass rendering, custom WGSL, and direct or indirect draws. - **Batched geometry and instances.** Geometry pools, instance buffers and GPU visibility reduce per-object submission work. Draw count still depends on meshes, materials and passes. - **GPU-resident integration.** Compute stages can write buffers that later rendering stages use. Buffers shared on the same device can avoid CPU readback and re-upload. Uploading a CPU typed array still transfers data to the GPU; it is not a zero-copy CPU-to-VRAM operation. - **Worker and headless support.** Use `OffscreenCanvas` for worker rendering, or render to an offscreen texture without a canvas. An existing `GPUDevice` can be adopted for interoperability. - **Reusable frame resources.** Buffer-backed APIs and prebuilt stage sequences support low- allocation frame loops. Applications remain responsible for their own allocations and uploads. ## Modules and features Modules are separate package subpaths so applications can import only what they use. Bundle size depends on the imported features and the application's bundler. | Import | Implemented features | Documentation | |--------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------| | `null-graph` | Device initialization/adoption, cameras, buffer and texture management, batches, compute stages, render passes, indirect drawing and headless rendering | [Usage](https://github.com/Vikas593-cloud/NullGraph/blob/master/docs/api/core.md) · [Reference](https://github.com/Vikas593-cloud/NullGraph/blob/master/docs/api/core-reference.md) | | `null-graph/geometry` | Vertex layouts, primitives, geometry builders, dynamic geometry, unified vertex/index pools, meshlets and LOD-chain construction | [Geometry](https://github.com/Vikas593-cloud/NullGraph/blob/master/docs/api/geometry.md) | | `null-graph/materials` | PBR, Lambert, Toon, Basic, Emissive and Matcap materials; composable WGSL shader builders | [Materials](https://github.com/Vikas593-cloud/NullGraph/blob/master/docs/api/materials.md) | | `null-graph/loaders` | GLB parsing, animation timelines, skeletal data, rigid/skinned animation baking and WGSL helpers for visible-instance animation palettes | [Loaders and animation](https://github.com/Vikas593-cloud/NullGraph/blob/master/docs/api/loaders.md) | | `null-graph/visibility` | GPU instance and meshlet culling, Hi-Z occlusion, normal-cone rejection, meshlet and instance LOD, indirect draws and app-defined instance vertex hooks | [Visibility](https://github.com/Vikas593-cloud/NullGraph/blob/master/docs/api/visibility.md) · [Shader reference](https://github.com/Vikas593-cloud/NullGraph/blob/master/docs/api/visibility-shader-reference.md) | | `null-graph/lights` | Buffer-backed lights with standard, tiled-forward and clustered-forward lighting | [Lights](https://github.com/Vikas593-cloud/NullGraph/blob/master/docs/api/lights.md) · [Shader reference](https://github.com/Vikas593-cloud/NullGraph/blob/master/docs/api/lights-shader-reference.md) | | `null-graph/shadows` | Cascaded directional shadows, punctual-light shadow atlas, cached tiles and caster culling integrated with visibility | [Shadows](https://github.com/Vikas593-cloud/NullGraph/blob/master/docs/api/shadows.md) · [Shader reference](https://github.com/Vikas593-cloud/NullGraph/blob/master/docs/api/shadows-shader-reference.md) | | `null-graph/environment` | Image-based diffuse/specular lighting, environment prefiltering, BRDF LUTs, irradiance volumes, GPU probe capture and parallax-corrected reflection probes | [Environment](https://github.com/Vikas593-cloud/NullGraph/blob/master/docs/api/environment.md) · [Probes](https://github.com/Vikas593-cloud/NullGraph/blob/master/docs/api/probes.md) | | `null-graph/post` | Explicit post-processing chains, reusable transient render targets, uniform arenas and through shader-layout contracts. Probe volumes support iterative bounce-light capture, while reflection probes supply local specular lighting. These are probe-based approximations, not ray-traced or guaranteed leak-free GI. Additional environment APIs are documented by feature rather than implementation order: - [Physical atmosphere](https://github.com/Vikas593-cloud/NullGraph/blob/master/docs/api/atmosphere.md) - [Aerial perspective and fog](https://github.com/Vikas593-cloud/NullGraph/blob/master/docs/api/aerial-perspective.md) - [Time of day](https://github.com/Vikas593-cloud/NullGraph/blob/master/docs/api/time-of-day.md) - [Night rendering](https://github.com/Vikas593-cloud/NullGraph/blob/master/docs/api/night-sky.md) - [Environment shader and buffer layouts](https://github.com/Vikas593-cloud/NullGraph/blob/master/docs/api/environment-shader-reference.md) - [Probe shader and buffer layouts](https://github.com/Vikas593-cloud/NullGraph/blob/master/docs/api/probes-shader-reference.md) ### GPU agents `AgentSystem` keeps live simulation state on the GPU and exposes explicit frame and lockstep scheduling. `RuleBrain` runs application WGSL; `MlpBrain` evaluates a supplied dense network. Each species can run its own brain (`setBrain(brain, { species })`), so rules and networks of different shapes can share one system, `MlpBrain.byGenome` holds a table of same-shape networks chosen per agent by the record's `genome` word, and `prepareBrain` compiles a brain ahead so that a switch compiles nothing. Neither policy is restricted to predator/prey or flocking behaviour. Applications define their observations, action semantics and additional simulation stages. The built-in movement and neighbour-query model is currently planar (XZ). The built-in network kernel runs small dense networks; adding a network does not train it. Larger models run through ONNX Runtime Web as an `OrtBrain`, from `null-graph/inference`: the app installs ONNX Runtime, an optional peer dependency, and its actions arrive one frame late in interactive frames. Training tooling is in the repository, not in the package. Neighbour scans have a configurable per-cell budget: crowded cells can omit candidates, and overflow-free operation is required for the documented same-device deterministic replay guarantee. See the [agents guide](https://github.com/Vikas593-cloud/NullGraph/blob/master/docs/api/agents.md) for supported shapes, buffer ownership, inspection and integration examples. ### Population policies and co-evolution building blocks The agent module provides reusable execution primitives for applications that evaluate multiple policies, evolve interacting populations, or compare current policies with historical opponents: - **Per-agent policy selection.** `MlpBrain.byGenome` stores same-shape networks in a GPU table; each agent's `genome` field selects its policy row. Candidate policies and archived policies can share a table without creating a separate brain for every network. - **Independent species policies.** `setBrain(brain, { species })` assigns brains per species, including networks of different shapes or a mixture of neural and WGSL rule policies. - **In-place policy updates.** `setWeights` replaces a network's weights, while `setRows` uploads contiguous packed rows to a genome-indexed table. Shapes and activations remain fixed; policy updates do not require rebuilding the brain. `prepareBrain` prepares a different brain ahead of a later switch. - **Explicit rollout scheduling.** Frame and lockstep execution let applications control simulation advancement, policy changes, and additional compute stages. GPU simulation buffers can feed rendering directly; inspection and evaluation readbacks remain explicit. These primitives support application-managed co-evolution and Hall-of-Fame-style (HoF) opponent sampling: applications retain historical networks, upload them as policy rows, and assign agents to current or archived policies. The library does not select archive members, define fitness, optimize weights, or guarantee that an evolved policy improves. Training algorithms, archive management, and evaluation protocols belong to application code or separate repository tooling, not the packaged agent runtime. ### Offline rendering and replay The repository's film tooling separates simulation from image production. A scene advances with a fixed timestep, declares GPU buffers to record, and supplies a rendering sequence. Record tracks without drawing, then replay them to render another camera, resolution or playback speed without rerunning the simulation. Export PNG frames or encode video through ffmpeg (60 fps by default). Full-buffer checkpoints and segment-level resume preserve committed work. Packed tracks can trade precision and sampling frequency for storage; they are not substitutes for exact continuation state. Offline output removes the real-time frame budget, not GPU memory limits or submission-safety checks. These are Node/Dawn tools in a repository checkout, not an npm package subpath or an automatic recorder for arbitrary browser applications. New scenes supply a small adapter; the recording core works with declared GPU buffers rather than requiring an agent simulation. See the [film setup and commands](./tools/film/README.md) and [general-purpose scene authoring guide](./tools/film/SCENE-AUTHORING.md). In the browser, `null-graph/film` films an application's own workload on the viewer's GPU, with no server: frame j is drawn at film time j / fps however long it takes, on an engine and target of its own (the app's preview is paused, not borrowed), encoded through WebCodecs and streamed to OPFS or a file the user picked. It has no tracks, checkpoints or resume; those stay with the Node tools. See the [film guide](./docs/api/film.md). ## Requirements and boundaries - **WebGPU is required.** There is no WebGL fallback. Optional GPU features are negotiated against the device; performance and available resource limits vary by adapter and host. - **This is a rendering library, not a complete game engine.** It does not provide a retained scene hierarchy, gameplay ECS, general rigid-body physics or automatic asset-to-scene assembly. - **Readbacks are explicit.** Picking, inspection and frame capture involve GPU-to-CPU transfers; GPU-resident frame paths need not perform those operations every frame. - **Text layout is not a shaping engine.** Complex-script shaping and bidirectional layout require additional application tooling. - **Scale is workload-dependent.** Geometry, passes, lights, shadows, query density, uploads and GPU limits all affect throughput. There is no universal entity-count or frame-time guarantee. ## Examples and validation - [Interactive demos](https://nullgraph.dev/) - [Demo source](https://github.com/Vikas593-cloud/NullGraph-Test-Engine) - [Application examples](https://github.com/Vikas593-cloud/NullGraph/blob/master/docs/agent/guide.md) - [Validation tools and workflow](https://github.com/Vikas593-cloud/NullGraph/blob/master/docs/agent/validation.md) From a repository checkout: ```sh npm install npm run build:lib npm run test:core npm run test:agents npm run test:agent-kit ``` Real-GPU harnesses run through Node/Dawn and headless Chrome: ```sh npm run test:gpu npm run test:gpu:browser npm run render -- test/gpu/scenes/quick-start.mjs --out cube.png npm run drive -- --serve . test/text-gpu/index.html --wait-for "passed|FAILED" ``` The GPU harnesses check numerical results and report uncaptured WebGPU errors. A passing run applies to the tested host and workload, not every GPU or application. Read the validation guide for setup, output reports and image inspection. `npm run drive` serves or opens a WebGPU page in headless Chrome, captures console output and screenshots, and can replay interaction steps from an actions file.
